In 1799, Tsar Paul I formalised the empire's Alaska claims by chartering the Russian-American Company. Modelled after the British East India Company, the for-profit venture didn't just control the fur trade; it now controlled all of Alaska as a corporate colony. But there was a problem: while the company was growing rich on sea otter pelts, the colonists were growing hungry because they couldn't farm in much of Alaska's frozen landscape. So, the Russian settlers sailed south in search of warmer climates and Spanish trading partners. California dreaming In April 1806, with his colony stalked by starvation and his crew decimated by scurvy, Russian-American Company director Nikolai Rezanov steered the prow of his ship, the Juno, into San Francisco Bay. As the brig limped towards Spain's northernmost California settlement, a Spanish soldier grabbed a megaphone and demanded the strange vessel identify itself. "Russia," a voice called back. It was a response the Spanish had been expecting for nearly 40 years. Though Spain claimed all of California starting in 1542, it didn't actually occupy it until 1769, after getting word that Russian fur traders were rapidly moving east across the Alaskan islands. To prevent Russian and British advancement, Spain created a chain of presidios (military outposts) along the coast, starting with San Diego. "The expansion of all of Alta [Upper] California, in many ways, was stimulated by the Russians," Lightfoot said. "The Spanish were nervous about the Russians coming south. So, the founding of San Diego, Santa Barbara, Monterey and San Francisco were a response to the Russians in Alaska." During Rezanov's six-week stay in San Francisco, the 42-year-old statesman secured enough food from the Spanish to save the starving Alaskan colonists by getting engaged to the 15-year-old daughter of San Francisco's Spanish commandant. As he sailed back through the Golden Gate, Rezanov realised that the entire northern coast of California was undefended and far sunnier than Siberia or Alaska, so he hatched a plan to extend Russian America into California. In 1812, after years of stealthily surveying the coast, 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskan hunters settled on a shelf-like plateau overlooking the Pacific on what is now Sonoma County's rugged coast. Here, close enough to the area's abundant sea otter population but far enough from the Spanish Empire's sparsely guarded northern frontier, they lived in a Siberian-designed settlement hewn from California redwoods under the tsar's double-eagle flag. Exploring Russian California Today, Russia's far-flung California colony remains a solitary, surreal place. Set 12 miles (19km) from the nearest town or mobile phone service, the weathered wooden remnants of a once-bustling settlement open onto a 180-degree view of the sea. In two days at the 3,400-acre Fort Ross State Historic Park, I counted 14 other visitors, and except for the occasional chime from the St Nicholas chapel, the only noise breaking the stillness was the waves crashing below the bluff. "There's a magical feel to Fort Ross," said Robin Joy Wellman, who worked as an interpreter with California State Parks for nearly 30 years. "It's something of a mystery, but once people discover it, they say it's one of the most beautiful places they've ever visited." The site's dramatic setting straddles the San Andreas fault, and the same earthquake that flattened San Francisco in 1906 also levelled much of the original wooden outpost. But detailed displays of the partially reconstructed fortress paint a vivid picture of frontier life in Russia's wild, wild East. The heart of the colony was the fort-like stockade, where a handful of high-ranking Russian soldiers, officers and company officials lived in barracks enclosed by a 12ft (3.6m) palisade. I followed Kimsey up the steps of two blockhouses armed with enough cannons to command the coast. He explained that while the Russians chose this natural overlook to defend against Spanish attacks, the two empires never actually clashed, and even depended on each other for survival. "The Russians and the Spanish were at the very far edges of their overstretched empires. They both needed things the other side could provide, so they traded illicitly," Kimsey said. In the warehouse, drying sea otter pelts worth $100 each (a year's salary for a Pennsylvania farmer at the time) destined for China, Europe and Spanish California would have hung from the rafters. Under the bulbous dome of one of the oldest Orthodox churches in the Western hemisphere, the little settlement gradually grew into a cosmopolitan colony, complete with banyas, bakeries and some 60 buildings. "It was a bustling, pluralistic mercantile village, with lots of languages and people from different homelands living together," Lightfoot said. "The stockade was just the tip of the iceberg. The real action was outside." Beyond the fort As Kimsey and I walked out of the palisade, he explained that as the colony expanded to include nearly 400 people by the 1830s, it became one of the most diverse places in California – and virtually everyone there worked for the Russian-American Company. Here, where the sloboda (village) once stood at the edge of the cape, paid Aleutian and Kodiak hunters lived with Native California women, mixed-race Russian and European Creoles married local Kashaya Pomo and Coast Miwok workers and people were buried next to each other at the Old Russian Cemetery up the hillside. Compared to other European colonies, it was also largely tolerant. "The Russians didn't come here to 'civilise' like the Spanish," said Kimsey, who serves as the tribal liaison for the area's Native communities. We then followed a steep path down to a crescent-shaped beach where coopers, carpenters and blacksmiths brought in by the Russian-American Company from as far afield as Finland and Hawaii once worked side by side. "This is where the first ocean-going ships in California were built," he said. It's also where the first bricks, glass and windmills in California were made. As workers crafted longboats, forged iron, cast brass and made metal, Fort Ross became the centre of manufacturing in California. The Russians traded these highly coveted goods with their Spanish and (later) Mexican neighbours in exchange for further provisions for their Alaskan settlements – and in doing so, they unwittingly helped their rivals settle California. More like this: This shallow-water cove was also where cargo boats and kayak-bound hunters would set off for the colony's main deep-water port 20 miles (35km) south in Rumyantsev (present-day Bodega Bay) and its sealing station off the coast of San Francisco on the Farallon Islands. As Fort Ross' footprint grew, so did the calls from within the Russian-American Company to heed Rezanov's recommendation of annexing North America's west coast for Russia. In 1821, Tsar Alexander I issued an imperial decree claiming Russian control over modern-day Oregon through Alaska. The US's soon-to-be sixth president, John Quincy Adams, swiftly objected and his warning to Russia that the Americas "are no longer subjects for any new European colonial establishments" established one of the most fundamental principles of US foreign policy: the Monroe Doctrine, which opposes foreign interference in the Western hemisphere. From the beach, Kimsey and I climbed a steep hill past the stockade to the orchard the Russians started with a single peach tree in 1814 and pushed open the gate. Of the hundreds of citrus trees and crops the Russians planted, only a single branch of a 200-year-old Capulin cherry survives. Yet, the Russians actually left a far greater agricultural legacy here than most people realise. "It was the Russians who planted the first grapes in [what is now] Sonoma County in 1817," said Megan Jones, Sonoma's official wine librarian. As Jones explained, while Sonoma is now considered "the birthplace of the modern American wine movement", Russian traders introduced the now-rare Mission grape to Sonoma and produced small batches of light red wine. For all its innovations, however, Fort Ross never succeeded in its two main goals: turning a profit and feeding hungry Alaskans. By the early 1820s, the Russian-American Company's Native Alaskan hunters had speared so many sea otters they wiped out the local population, and a combination of heavy coastal fog and rampant rodents yielded just 13 tonnes of wheat annually between 1826 and 1833. When the British-run Hudson's Bay Company agreed to supply Russian Alaska with provisions from its Pacific Northwest settlements starting in 1839, it was the beginning of the end for Tsarist California. Two years later, a Swiss emigrant named John Sutter purchased Fort Ross' buildings and assets from the Russians for $30,000. He cannibalised parts of the structures to create his new settlement in Sacramento. Seven years after the Russians sailed back to Alaska, a chance discovery on Sutter's property ignited the California Gold Rush. Russia's California legacy Today, reminders of California's Tsarist past are still scattered across the Golden State as you drive north from San Francisco. One of the city's most famous neighbourhoods, Russian Hill, gets its name from the graves of Russian-American Company sailors discovered there during the Gold Rush (look for a plaque near 1120 Vallejo Street). A historical marker at Bodega Bay shows where Russians set sail for their Alaskan capital, Novo-Arkhangelsk (present-day Sitka). And more than a million people visit the Russian River Valley each year to splash, hike and taste some of the US's best wines. "The Russians called this river Slavyanka, and it's one of the main arteries they used to exploit the area," said Suki Waters, a Kashaya Pomo descendant and the owner of WaterTreks, which leads eco-tours along the Russian River. As we kayaked past harbour seals and migrating pelicans, she recounted stories from her great-great-grandmother, who was alive when the Russians sailed in. "Fort Ross was a seasonal fishing village called Metini for thousands of years," she said. "When the Russians first came, the Elders called them the 'Undersea People', because from high on the bluff, it looked like they rose out from under the ocean." Later that afternoon, I walked back through Fort Ross' Cyrillic signs, stockade and sloboda towards a lone bench at the edge of that bluff. Peering across the Pacific, I wondered how many days it would take to reach Russia. But as a distant chime from the chapel echoed in the air, I was reminded of something Wellman told me. "The fact that a little part of Russia was right here in California is amazing. Why would we ever want to forget that?" --

item.title: Five unwritten rules for visiting Spain
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 4.83
'Paella is just for lunch' and other unwritten rules for visiting Spain Spain is famous for its laid-back lifestyle, but beneath the long lunches and late nights are social codes that shape everyday life. Our expert explains how to read them. While Spain is beloved for its beautiful beaches, romantic architecture and delicious food culture, one of its strongest draws is its famously relaxed pace. No hay prisa ("no rush") and tranquilo ("relax") are oft-uttered phrases here; meals are drawn out and nightlife lasts until morning. Even non-Spanish speakers know the meaning of siesta. Get to know your expert Jill Petzinger is a British journalist and professional travel advisor who specialises in Spain and Southern Europe. Based in Valencia since 2021, she has travelled extensively throughout Spain to explore the many regional cuisines and cultural traditions. But "relaxed" doesn't mean there's no order. Beneath Spain's easy-going surface are silent social codes that shape everything from how people queue to how they structure their days. Instinctive rather than explicitly stated, Spain's unwritten social rules are often based on respect for regional identity, a belief that life is best lived sociably in public and a historical need to work with, not against, the searing Sun. Locals might not say them out loud, but that doesn't make them any less important to learn. From relinquishing your personal space to skipping paella at dinner, here are five unwritten rules that will help you understand Spain from the inside. 1. Trust the invisible queue Try to order at a covered market, pharmacy, bakery, bar or local shop in Spain and you'll typically find people standing around randomly, no clear line in sight. It may seem confusing to the outsider, but there's a deeply ingrained system at play, rooted in a cultural preference for interaction, informality and social trust. "Queues" in Spain do indeed exist, but they are typically spread-out crowds rather than prim lines because of space constraints in small premises or market aisles; standing where it's most convenient solves the issue. But how do you know when it's your turn? What to do: When you arrive, approach the closest person and ask "¿Quién es el último?" (Who's last?) or simply "¿El último?" They will point to whomever is. Once you know who's last, you're free to walk along the displays and peruse what to buy without losing your place. But stay alert: you will get asked "¿El último?", too. 2. Don't assume the meal is over when it's over You've just had the last bites of Spanish tortilla and the last drops of Rioja. But before you ask for the bill, look around. The tables next to you, strewn with empty glasses and crumpled napkins, may look like they've finished too, but they're just entering another phase: the ritual known as la sobremesa. Literally translated as "over the table", la sobremesa is the hour (or hours) after the meal when everyone settles in for a long conversation. It may involve another round of coffee or drinks, but there's no pressure: la sobremesa is all about enjoying each other's company. The tradition is thought to stretch back to the agricultural past, when families sat around the table after lunch as it was still too hot return to the fields immediately. Most Spaniards may no longer till the fields, but the sobremesa continues its role in maintaining relationships. The joy of enjoying each meal for as long as possible has never gone out of style. What to do: Simply relax, put away your phone and keep chatting away. Waiters are used to letting people enjoy their conversations, so just raise a hand to ask for the bill when you're (really) ready to leave. And feel free to linger even longer. 3. Follow the Sun Spain's famously late rhythm can bewilder visitors, with dinners that last until midnight and shops that close for hours after lunch. But there's a logic behind the seemingly languorous rhythm. In Spain, people work with, not against, the Sun. Historically, Spanish farmers started the day early to get their work done before the Sun grew too hot, saving lunch until they were through. Then, in the 1940s, General Franco moved the clocks forward to align with Nazi Germany. Though the country now found itself in the Central European time zone, many stuck to the traditional solar schedule: lunch at 13:00 became lunch at 14:00 as the sun reached its zenith an hour later than before, and dinner happened later, too, as the light now lasted longer. More like this: In Spain, the workday is also slightly longer than the EU average: 36.3 hours per week versus 35.9 hours. Perhaps that's why Spain's famous "siesta" is increasingly less the norm, since 80% of its population now lives in cities. Unable to head home at lunchtime and have a nap, workers now often return to the office or use the post-lunch time to tackle chores. What to do: Shape your day around avoiding the worst of the afternoon Sun between 13:00 and 18:00 – a light breakfast. Check shop hours to avoid slogging through the heat to a shuttered destination, and keep in mind that only tourist restaurants open at 19:00. If you can hold off until 20:30 or 21:00 you'll be able to eat at better establishments. Consider a strategic siesta to help you stave off the hunger, or prepare for a long night. 4. Make room for the crowd Spain is a tactile nation, where touching an arm for emphasis, greeting with hugs and (lots of) kisses, bumping shoulders in a bar and standing close to strangers in a line are all everyday aspects of social behaviour – though they can surprise visitors from places with stricter norms around personal proximity. Furthermore, whether you find yourself in the city or the village, Spanish social life has traditionally been lived in public places like plazas, bars and streets. These shared spaces can get quite closely packed, meaning you end up very close to your neighbours by default. What to do: Don't automatically read physical closeness as rudeness. Stake out your own (little) space but accept that you'll still catch accidental bumps and jostles in busy areas. If you need to squeeze past someone, a simple "perdón" (sorry) suffices, and almost always elicits "no pasa nada" (no problem) from the other person. 5. Don't order paella for dinner or sangria at a bar Thanks to Spain's thriving tourist industry, you'll find the same supposed Spanish staples – sangria, paella and tapas – wherever you go. But Spain is a huge country, with 17 autonomous communities on the mainland, and an equal number of regional cuisines. Traditionally, people ate what was produced locally, and that love for and loyalty towards regional identity when it comes to food is still strong today. Embrace the opportunity to enjoy the beloved dishes of the city you're visiting. Paella is revered as a native dish of Valencia and Catalonia, but wherever you try it, do it like the Spanish and order it just at lunchtime, as it is considered a heavy meal to digest. Tapas bars will serve regional specialties depending on the city, but the sheer creative variety of pintxos is best enjoyed in their Basque homeland. If you're in Madrid in the colder months, don't miss the famous meaty chickpea cocido stew; enjoy gazpacho in Andalusia and most of Spain in the summer. Year-round, consider swerving the sangria. Locals do drink it, but it's not regarded a bar drink: it's more commonly consumed as a punch at parties. What to do: If a restaurant has a photo menu, it will likely be a tourist trap. To explore regional dishes, try a three-course menú del dia in local restaurants during weekdays. These menus are dying out in Spain partly because of shorter lunch breaks and the rise of new, trendier eateries, so look out for places full of locals with daily chalkboard menus, generally indicating fresh, seasonal food. To drink at the bar like a local, order the nationally adored tinto de verano, a mix of red wine and lemonade that contains no hard liquor, or tiny caña draft beers, which stay colder longer. --

item.title: The Nazi shipwrecks emerging from the Danube
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.27
The Nazi shipwrecks emerging from the Danube As the Danube shrinks under extreme heat, the river is revealing a startling remnant of Europe's wartime past. This month, record-low water levels on the Danube have exposed at least 20 German warships near Prahovo in eastern Serbia. Rusted hulls and broken masts are emerging from the river – the remains of a Nazi Black Sea fleet deliberately scuttled during World War Two. Wrecks have surfaced during previous droughts, but this summer's extreme heat and drought have brought dozens of vessels back into view. Some are believed to contain weapons and explosives, turning this stretch of one of Europe's great cruising rivers into an eerie, visible battlefield. For travellers cruising along the Danube this summer, the falling water is revealing a landscape – and history – normally hidden beneath the river. Eighty-two years beneath the Danube The story of how they got there begins more than eight decades ago. By 1944, German forces were retreating on the Eastern Front as the Soviets advanced through the region, leaving a fleet of around 200 Nazi Black Sea vessels stranded in what was an area rapidly falling under Soviet control. The Danube offered an escape route, but the Iron Gates – a narrow and historically treacherous stretch of the river – created a bottleneck. In September 1944, German Rear Admiral Paul-Willy Zieb ordered more than 200 vessels scuttled as the Red Army closed in. The ships were deliberately sunk to prevent their capture and obstruct the Soviet advance. Most have remained submerged beneath the river ever since, partly because many still contain unexploded ordnance and pose a hazard to navigation. Serbia has launched an estimated €30m removal programme to remove some of the vessels, but progress has been slow because clearing the riverbed safely is complex. For travellers, it's a striking sight along Europe's second-longest river, which stretches roughly 2,850km (1,770 miles) across 10 countries and centuries full of falling empires and shifting allegiances. Kenneth Reece, a travel planner who recently cruised the lower Danube aboard the Avalon Passion, says reminders of the region's turbulent history surrounded them throughout their trip. "We visited medieval fortresses, heard stories about life under communism and dictatorship, learned about the wars that have shaped this region and travelled through places where some of that history is still within living memory," Reece said. "Hearing about the WWII-era German shipwrecks beneath the Danube added another layer… The history wasn't only in museums or monuments. Some of it was quite literally beneath us." How to see what the Danube has revealed Nazi shipwrecks – Prahovo, Serbia: At least 20 wrecks have been visible from the riverbank at Prahovo, near the Serbian-Romanian border, this summer. Some are still believed to contain weapons or explosives, so they should be viewed from the bank rather than approached. Visibility will change as river levels rise and fall. Woolly mammoth remains – Ruse, Bulgaria: Bones exposed near the village of Ryahovo in July have been recovered by specialists from the Regional History Museum in Ruse. After conservation and study, they're expected to go on display at the museum, about 30km from where they were found. What else the river is revealing The Nazi ships aren't the only remnants emerging as the Danube falls. This August, receding water has also exposed a German army Wehrmacht motorcycle in Budapest and a 1,543lb British bomb near Virt, Slovakia, which was later safely detonated. At Gigen in Bulgaria, falling water has revealed the remains of the ancient Constantine Bridge, while near Ryahovo, archaeologists unearthed woolly mammoth tusks and bones dating back thousands of years. "For archaeologists, these moments are extremely valuable," Pavel Popov of the Regional Historical Museum in Pleven told Reuters. "It gives us a rare opportunity to observe, document and study it in its real environment." Droughts and fluctuating water levels are not new to the Danube. Europe is the fastest-warming continent, according to the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service, warming at more than twice the global average. Rising temperatures are intensifying heat extremes and altering rainfall patterns, contributing to repeated low-water events that disrupt navigation along the river. "The Danube was revealing warnings from our past while, at the same time, perhaps giving us a warning about our future," Reece said. What low water means for travellers The consequences are already being felt by visitors to the region. This summer's low waters have forced Danube cruise operators to cancel sailings, change itineraries, transfer passengers between ships and use coaches to bypass unnavigable sections of the river. More like this: Yet the changing river can also transform what travellers encounter along the way. "We never realised that we would sail directly over the sunken German warships," said Suzanna Fulton, who recently cruised on the Viking Honir. "It was humbling and quite honestly, a cool experience." Reece said seeing evidence of the Danube's wartime history made the beauty and peacefulness of the river feel more poignant. "Today, you can sit on the deck of a river cruise ship with a glass of wine and watch these beautiful countries pass by, but this same landscape has witnessed war, fascism, oppression and tremendous human suffering," he said. "I think that's what stayed with me most. The Danube wasn't simply taking us through Europe. In many ways, it was taking us through Europe's history." --

item.title: Inside the places that shaped Dolly Parton
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.21
'Everything about her was East Tennessee': The places that shaped Dolly Parton From her Appalachian childhood to Nashville and Dollywood, a journey through the Tennessee she loved – and transformed in return. On a sunny day on 24 June 2026, hundreds of travellers, locals and Dolly Parton fans from across the US gathered in the small rural community of Cornersville, less than an hour's drive south of Nashville, for the unveiling of her Tennessean Travel Stop. It was the country star's last public appearance before her death just two months later. Wearing her signature fringe and rhinestones and a grin as bright as that Tennessee morning, Parton cut the ribbon and welcomed travellers to the new roadside stop, complete with a Southern meat-and-three restaurant, live music and – of course – a Dolly-themed gift shop. It was a fitting final chapter for an artist whose life and career were inseparable from Tennessee. From crooning about the Smoky Mountains to investing in rural East Tennessee where she grew up, Parton spent decades sharing her home state with the world – and transforming it in return. Explore Parton's Tennessee mountain home In 1964, US President Lyndon B Johnson launched the War on Poverty, a federal effort to reduce poverty and expand economic opportunity across the United States. Southern Appalachia, one of the nation's poorest regions, was thrust into the national spotlight. Media portrayals often depicted its residents as backward and destitute, reinforcing the caricature of the "hillbilly", a stereotype that had persisted since the 19th Century. But when Dolly Rebecca Parton came into the spotlight, this daughter of Appalachia who grew up in a two-room cabin with 11 brothers and sisters offered the world a different view of her home: one of joy, dignity and talent. Follow Dolly Parton's story across Tennessee Sevierville: See the bronze statue of Parton outside the Sevier County Courthouse and The Pines, where she performed for a paying audience for the first time at just 10 years old. RCA Studio B, Nashville: Visit the legendary recording studio on Music Row where Dolly Parton and other iconic artists like Elvis Presley recorded some of their greatest hits. The Country Music Hall of Fame, Nashville: A must-visit Nashville institution that chronicles the history of country music through artefacts, exhibits and the stories of the artists who trailblazed the genre. Dollywood, Pigeon Forge: Set in the Smoky Mountains that Parton loved so dearly, Dollywood takes guests on a journey through the singer's roots, from an exact replica of her childhood two-room cabin to the Dolly Parton Experience, which displays childhood memorabilia. "Dolly Parton told a new story about Appalachia that was rooted in her very particular experience," said Dr Jessie Wilkerson, a history professor and Appalachian scholar at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. "Yes, her family was poor, but they weren't desperate or hopeless, and they took care of one another. There was a lot of love and beauty in the place where she grew up, and so we get a different story about Appalachia through her." In the title track of her 1973 album, My Tennessee Mountain Home, Parton describes her Appalachian home as "peaceful as a baby's sigh". The landscape around her childhood home on the edge of the Great Smoky Mountains, along with Appalachia's storytelling traditions and bluegrass heritage, inspired much of Parton's music. In Great Smoky Mountains National Park, a blue-grey mist that gives the Smokies its name settles over the peaks and valleys and waterfalls tumble through the forest. The 522,000-acre expanse is threaded with hiking trails and scenic overlooks, with autumn bringing a canvas of brilliant jewel tones and spring a kaleidoscope of wildflowers to the lower slopes. The landscape was a reoccurring muse, from the mountain blooms that inspired her 1987 ballad Wildflowers to the fog-covered peaks evoked in Blue Smoke, the title track of her 2014 album, and the pastoral idyll captured in My Tennessee Mountain Home. In nearby Sevierville, the main town serving rural Locust Ridge, where Parton grew up, the region's pride in its local legend is evident. A bronze statue on the courthouse lawn depicts her as a young girl playing guitar. Down the street is the Wings of Wander mural, inspired by her hit song Love Is Like a Butterfly, and the Red's Cafe mural, another larger-than-life depiction of Parton as a child, this time getting a cheeseburger from her favourite childhood restaurant. "People in East Tennessee really, really adore her, and it's something that's been important for the region to have someone who's really proud of coming from there, and who's a positive representation of Appalachia, when historically the representations of the region are the opposite," Wilkerson said. Retracing Parton's path in Nashville On the day Parton graduated from high school in 1964, she boarded a Greyhound bus headed west for the neon lights of Nashville. In a letter home shortly after arriving, feeling homesick and uncertain, she wrote, "Nashville isn't what I thought it was gonna be, but I think I'll like it once I get used to it." "When she came to Nashville, she came with a very distinct East Tennessee identity and made that very clear in both her music and her accent," said Robert K Oermann, co-author of her memoir Dolly Parton: Songteller, My Life in Lyrics and a longtime collaborator. "Everything about her was East Tennessee and mountain, and I think that was the message she brought to Nashville." Nashville looks very different today from when Parton first stepped off that bus 62 years ago, but visitors can still trace Parton's path from her early days fresh out of Sevier County to her rise as a country music icon who never lost the Appalachian sound of home even as she became one of Nashville's biggest stars. On Music Row, the city's historic record-industry district, visitors can step inside RCA Studio B where a blue X marks "The Sweet Spot" where Parton recorded hits including Jolene and I Will Always Love You – both of which she wrote on the same day. Nearby, the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum is featuring Dolly Parton: Journey of a Seeker, an exhibition spanning her career and featuring memorabilia like her Gibson five-string banjo and handwritten music drafts. A few blocks away, the historic Ryman Auditorium is where a 13-year-old Parton made her Grand Ole Opry debut in 1959 and earned three encores. Murals of Parton dot the city in her honour, museum exhibits display her stage costumes and in the wake of her passing, fans have left flowers on her star on the Music City Walk of Fame. Visiting Parton's Appalachia Nashville, however, was never the end of Parton's journey. The further her career carried her from the mountains to Nashville and eventually Hollywood, the more firmly she seemed to plant her roots at the centre of her story. In 1982, she told Barbara Walters in an interview about her dream of opening a "mountain Disneyland" in her Appalachian home region. More like this: Today, that "mountain Disneyland" is Dollywood, a major tourist destination in Sevier County that invites visitors into the version of Appalachia Parton spent her career sharing with the world. Beyond the thrill rides and water park are shows featuring Parton's music, some performed by members of her own family. But to Parton, Dollywood was also a way to give back to the mountains and the community that nurtured her. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.61
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: Pommes Dauphine
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.05
Pommes dauphine (classic French potato puffs) are part of the vast lexicon of potato dishes rarely seen outside of the country. Think of the bite-size clouds as fried mashed potatoes, only lighter and more magical. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City sticks to the traditional method, mixing equal parts pâte à choux with a purée of roasted potatoes. You’ll spoon the mixture into hot oil to create golden, crisp yet airy puffs. Serve as a chic appetizer or party snack paired with aioli or whatever dipping sauce your heart desires—or, in true French fashion, alongside a hearty steak or roast chicken as an impressive side. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; Ratatouille; and Dover Sole Meunière. Ingredients 1 4 1 ⅔ 2–3 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Sprinkle coarse salt over a rimmed baking sheet to cover (aim for a ¼"–½" thick layer). Nestle 1 lb. large Yukon Gold potatoes (2–3) into the salt and roast in oven until a knife pierces through flesh with little resistance, about 30 minutes. Step 2Remove from oven and, working quickly so potatoes remain hot, peel with a paring knife and halve. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl; set aside. Step 3Bring 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ⅔ cup water to a simmer in a medium saucepan over high heat, stirring with a stiff heatproof spatula or sturdy rubber spatula to help melt butter and dissolve salt. Immediately reduce heat to medium; add ⅔ cup all-purpose flour all at once and stir quickly until most of the flour is absorbed. Cook, stirring vigorously and breaking up pockets of flour as needed, until a thin film forms on bottom and sides of pan and dough comes together into a single mass, 2–3 minutes. (It should look glossy and feel buttery and smooth.) Remove from heat and let sit in pan until no longer hot but still warm, about 3 minutes. Step 4Add 2 large eggs to mixture one at a time, mixing until incorporated after each addition. Pâte à choux should be thick, glossy, and fall off spatula in a V-shape. If it’s too thick, stir in another 1 large egg. Add dough to reserved potatoes and stir to combine; season with kosher salt. Step 5Pour peanut oil into a medium Dutch oven or large heavy saucepan fitted with thermometer to come 3" up sides (about 8 cups). Heat over medium-high until thermometer registers 360°. Reduce heat to medium (you want to maintain the temperature). Using a spoon lightly coated in oil and working in batches of 6–8, spoon irregular amounts of batter into pot. Fry, turning often, until golden brown all over, about 4 minutes. Using a spider or slotted spoon, transfer to a rimmed baking sheet lined with paper towels to drain and immediately season with kosher salt. Repeat process with remaining batter, adjusting heat as needed to maintain temperature. Transfer pommes dauphine to a platter to serve.

item.title: Pommes Purée (French Mashed Potatoes)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.56
Pommes purée is France’s answer to mashed potatoes. But instead of simply mashing the spuds, they get passed through a food mill and a tamis (a large fine-mesh drum) to make them as smooth as satin sheets. Think of them as the fancier, more luxe version of the comfort food classic. Here, chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, takes inspiration from chef Joël Robuchon’s famous version, adding a wealth of milk and butter to the potatoes for a truly decadent result. You can serve them as a comforting side next to roast chicken or seared steak, elevating any dinner into a bistro-worthy affair. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 2 1 1 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 lb. 4 oz. large Yukon gold potatoes (5–7) in a large pot and pour in water to cover by about 2". Season generously with kosher salt and bring to a boil. Cook until potatoes are fork-tender, 20–25 minutes. Step 2Meanwhile, heat 1 cup whole milk in a small saucepan over low heat and keep warm. Step 3Drain potatoes. Working quickly so they remain hot, peel potatoes with a paring knife and cut into pieces. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl, then pass through tamis onto a sheet of parchment paper, pressing with a heatproof rubber spatula. Step 4Transfer potato purée to a small pot or large saucepan and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until dried out a little and steaming, about 3 minutes. Gradually pour in warm milk, stirring constantly until smooth and spoonable (you might not need all of the milk). Remove from heat and add 1 cup (2 sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced, a few pieces at a time, whisking after each addition until melted and combined before adding more. Taste pommes purée and season with salt as needed.

item.title: Pommes Anna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.94
Pommes Anna is a French potato cake made of thinly sliced potatoes cooked in nothing more than butter. While humble in its ingredients, the cake is as dramatic as can be. Baked in a skillet, it gets turned out to reveal a graphic spiral of spuds on top. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, keeps things classic in her recipe, layering paper-thin slices of potatoes with plenty of butter to create a multilayered potato cake that’s crisp on the outside and tender in the center. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 5 1¼ ½ Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Slice 5 lb. large Yukon gold potatoes (10–15), peeled, lengthwise on a mandoline set to 1-mm thickness. Step 2Brush a large high-sided skillet with some of 1¼ cups clarified butter to coat. Cut a round of parchment paper to fit bottom of pan and place in pan. Brush parchment with more clarified butter. Using cutter and working with a few slices stacked together at a time, punch out enough rounds to fill bottom of pan. Arrange slices around sides of pan, overlapping slightly, to create a circle (make sure slices are compact and tight). Repeat process, creating concentric circles, until you have an even layer covering entire bottom of pan. Drizzle with some clarified butter and generously season with kosher salt. Repeat process (no need to cut potatoes into rounds), creating more layers, until all of the potatoes slices and clarified butter have been used. Dot ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, sliced, over final layer of potatoes. Step 3Cover pan with a lid or foil and bake potatoes until tender, 50–55 minutes. Uncover and bake until deep golden brown in spots, 45–55 minutes more. Let cool slightly, then place a plate upside down over pan. Holding plate and pan together, carefully turn over in one swift motion to invert pommes Anna onto plate. Remove pan.

item.title: Crispy Potato Kugel
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.76
When many people hear “kugel,” visions of a sweet egg noodle casserole first come to mind, delighting many and confusing others. Savory potato kugel, however, is almost universally pleasing. Landing in between a latke and a Spanish tortilla in flavor and texture, potato kugel is, like all kugels, a baked casserole common in the Ashkenazi Jewish culinary tradition. Filled with grated potato, onion, and egg, it’s a no-brainer side dish for high holidays, like Rosh Hashanah and Passover, or weekly shabbat, but it’s welcome on the table any day alongside meaty mains such as braised brisket or roast chicken. Where latke mixture must be squeezed extremely dry to fry into crisp pancakes, potato kugel’s creamy texture comes from leaving some of that liquid in the mix. Using mayonnaise in the filling—and to grease the pan—instead of traditional schmaltz or olive oil helps ensure the kugel bakes off moist, rich, and crisp—never dry or greasy. Fat wedges of potato kugel are excellent topped with a dollop of sour cream and a sprinkle of chopped chives (but, of course, if you’re keeping kosher and serving meat alongside, you’ll want skip the dairy). Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours - Yield 10–12 servings Ingredients 4 3 1 3¼ 3 3 1 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Brush bottom and sides of a 9"-diameter springform pan, metal cake pan, or cast-iron skillet with 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise. (If using a springform pan, place a baking sheet underneath rack to catch any drips.) Fill a medium bowl with water. Peel 3 lb. russet potatoes (about 4 large) and quarter; place in bowl of water. Quarter 1 medium onion. Using a food processor fitted with a coarse grating disk, grate potatoes and onion. (Alternatively, grate on the large holes of a box grater.) Step 2Transfer potato mixture to a large colander or fine-mesh sieve set over a large bowl. Sprinkle with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to combine. Let sit 5 minutes to allow excess liquid to drain. Step 3Using your hands, press out more liquid from potato mixture (it should not be totally dry). Transfer colander to a plate. Gently pour out liquid from bowl, leaving behind any white starch accumulated at the bottom. Step 4Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture. Step 5Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture.

item.title: Best Dutch Ovens for Braising, Baking, and Beyond (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.17
Over the past few decades, I'd argue that the Dutch oven has eclipsed the stand mixer as the most crucial piece of kitchen equipment for making a kitchen feel like a home kitchen. Is it because they're heavy and expensive? It it because couples always put them on their wedding registries? Is it because you can make soup in them and soup is comforting and feels homey and there's something to that? Not entirely sure. I can say though, that setting down one of these colorful, enameled hunks of cast iron onto a stove is akin to dropping an anchor. By committing to making a Sunday braise in a Dutch oven you're saying, “ This is my home, and because it's my home, I'm gonna make the entire place, and my clothes, smell like ragú.” But which to buy? I've spent years and years thinking about this, because the question of what the best Dutch oven is, is a question that requires a lot of caveats and asterisks. Yes, there are certainly some design and quality metrics that help distinguish the Staubs and Le Creusets from Amazon Basics, but the bottom line is: Every Dutch oven on the market will deliver an extremely similar cooking performance. What it all comes down to is quality and design. Our top picks - The best Dutch oven overall: Le Creuset Signature Round 5.5-Quart Dutch Oven - The other best Dutch oven: Staub 5.5-Quart Cocotte - The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Cheap Dutch ovens work just fine, but their affordability comes at the cost of quality control. Budget Dutch ovens consistently feature manufacturer defects, chipping, and thinner enamel layers that can lead to accelerated wear and rusting. As for design, while there are some practical advantages that some have over others, a lot of it comes down to subjective preferences. There are two people who have worked on this test over the years and we have vehemently disagreed with each other over the top spot, though, to be clear both of our choices are great Dutch ovens. I'll get more into the two that always tussle for the top spot, as well as the most well-designed budget picks that also come with lifetime warranties. Keep reading to learn about how I and my team have tested Dutch ovens over the years, how to keep the enamel in tip-top shape, and which brands didn’t make the short list. New in this update: I added reviews for the Crockpot, Goldilocks, and Müeller Dutch ovens, and moved Le Creuset into a clear top spot. A Beautiful, easy-to-handle Dutch oven with a light interior: Le Creuset Signature Enameled Cast-Iron 5.5-Quart Round Dutch Oven Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Relatively lightweight - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Light interior enamel will show wear more readily than dark enamel Specs Interior enamel: Light and smooth Available sizes: 2-qt., 4.5-qt., 5.5-qt., 7.25-qt., 9-qt., 13.75-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 11.6 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: We’ve been recommending Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens for as long as we’ve been recommending Dutch ovens. So if you have your heart set on one of these iconic pieces and you’re wondering whether it’s still a wise investment, the answer is a resounding yes. Le Creuset’s smooth, sand-colored interior enamel produced a beautiful, even sear—and the light enamel makes it easy to keep an eye on browning and fond development. Le Creuset’s 5.5-quart Dutch oven also weighs about a pound less than Staub’s with thin loop handles that are easy to grip with or without oven mitts. The lighter weight comes courtesy of noticeably thinner cast iron, but it’s still thick enough to offer wonderful heat retention. Le Creuset Dutch ovens typically have a wider cooking surface and lower sides. This means more space for searing meats for braising—an essential Dutch oven task. A few years ago Le Creuset began offering metal knobs on its Dutch ovens, which was a meaningful upgrade as the old phenolic knobs could melt if you tried to do something like use your Dutch oven to bake bread at 450℉, it would melt. Then there is the manufacturing quality. Le Creuset is a century-old French brand, and though some of its cookware and tableware is now made in other countries, all of the enameled cast-iron cookware—including the Dutch ovens—is still made in the original manufacturing facility in Fresnoy-le-Grand, France. And while we know from experience with inherited pieces that the chip-resistant enamel can last a lifetime (with proper care, of course), Le Creuset Dutch ovens do come with a limited lifetime warranty. What I’d leave: When covered at a boil, the Le Creuset may sputter at the edges a little. If you choose a Dutch oven with light-colored interior enamel, and cook in it often, you should expect some gradual discoloration. If you’re intent on keeping it pristine, you may jeopardize the lifespan of the enamel. Abrasive cleaners can wear the seal off of it and lead to even more staining. A gorgeous, top-notch Dutch oven with a dark interior: Staub Round Cocotte Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Dark, textured cooking surface browns quicker and hides stains - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Lint from some dish towels can catch on interior enamel Specs Interior enamel: Dark and textured Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 12.57 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: In terms of craftsmanship and price, Staub’s Dutch oven, which the brand calls a “cocotte,” is in no ways inferior to the Le Creuset. Both are premium enameled cast-iron round Dutch ovens with high-quality chip-resistant enamel, and both heat and sear evenly. Interior enamel is a matter of preference, and the Bon Appétit staff is divided on this matter. The Staub's dark, textured enamel interior does absorb more thermal energy which is helpful for producing an intense sear. The enamel also also has a rougher surface texture, which Staub claims helps distribute fat beneath ingredients to encourage browning and an easier release. While there is some truth to this, the relationship between surface texture and food sticking isn't cut and dry. Many other variables, such as temperature, time, fat volume, technique, and the type of food, have an impact as well. As Robert J. Macfarlane, a materials scientist at MIT pointed out to me, surface texture can increase surface area, which combined with poor technique and inadequate oil can actually make sticking worse. All of that to say: This Dutch oven produces a great sear, but the added benefits of Staub's dark textured enamel aren't significant enough to champion over classic light enamel. One thing that is for sure though—the dark interior won’t show discoloration like a light one will. Looking beyond the enamel, the Staub's lid is well-designed, preventing liquid sputters when shut at a boil. The bumps underneath are supposed to distribute condensation, though we've never observed a difference in the end product between Dutch ovens with bumpy lids and Dutch ovens without. I prefer the flat lid over a curved one, as you can invert the lid and stack the Dutch oven for easy storage. Yes, it’s pricey, but with proper care it will be something your kids fight over once you're gone. Like Le Creuset, Staub is a French cookware brand (now owned by Zwilling), its Dutch ovens are still manufactured in France, and they maintain an exceedingly high bar for what ends up on store shelves. One of the big reasons for the price is the high volume of units they reject along the assembly line (cast-iron is a material that evades easy refinement). This scrutiny means that your Dutch oven will almost certainly be free of surface defects and chips. If you do find any, definitely reach out to them, as Staub also offers a limited lifetime warranty on its enameled cast iron. What I'd leave: The dark enamel makes it a bit harder to monitor browning, which might be intimidating for greener cooks. Also, the Staub is heavier than the Le Creuset and the handles are slightly smaller, but it's a pretty negligible distinction if you're trying to champion one excellent product over the other. The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Pros and cons Pros: - Generous surface area - Large handles - Affordable - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Too young a brand to judge longevity Specs Interior enamel: White Available sizes: 6 qt Weight (5.5-qt. size): 13.7 lb. Multiple color options: Blue, red, green. Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Lifetime warranty What I loved: As a relative newcomer to the cookware space, Goldilocks has consistently produced well-made, affordable cookware. It's clear that they pay attention to design, and that is evident in their Dutch oven. This Dutch oven was a pleasure to cook with, and had no apparent defects in design or performance. The design prioritizes width over height, something we appreciate for searing and browning meat before a braise. In fact is one of the widest round Dutch ovens relative to its height and volume. But rest assured it fits fine over standard burners. Its handles are also nice and large, making them easy to grab and maneuver, even with thick oven mitts on. It is still more expensive than some of the better known and more popular cheaper models made by Amazon and Lodge, and we can't yet speak to the longterm longevity of the enamel coating since this is still a newer product. However, I'd argue that the physical dimensions themselves also make this a superior choice to previous budget picks. What I'd leave: Again, I can't yet speak toward longevity yet so we will update this test in the future. Beyond that, it is slightly heavier than the winners, and also is extremely limited in size and color offerings. However, 6 quarts is the median ideal size for a Dutch oven. How we tested Dutch ovens Steam test We also tested the lids by conducting steam tests and filling each one about halfway with water that we brought to a rolling boil in order to see if the lid would prevent spattering. Ideally, the lid will release some steam at such high temperatures, but contain water in its scalding, liquid form. Form evaluation Most importantly, we evaluated the physical dimensions of each Dutch oven: how much they weigh relative to their size, how large their handles are, and their height-to-width ratio. We also do longterm testing on winning models to evaluate issues with wear and longevity. Both the Test Kitchen team and the product reviews team use Dutch ovens on a regular basis, which helps inform our testing as well. What we looked for in a Dutch oven Durable enamel Without the kind of serious long-term testing we’re able to do with the Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens many of us have owned for years, it’s hard to tell just how durable a Dutch oven’s porcelain enamel will be. But sometimes really cheap enamel will have small chips or pinholes right out of the box. You can also look at customer reviews; most will have at least a few reporting enamel damage. If it’s a small percentage of reviews, it’s likely a manufacturing defect, but if a disproportionate amount of reviewers complain about chipped or damaged enamel, it’s likely a durability issue. Comfortable handles Even when they’re empty, Dutch ovens are pretty heavy—hell, the lids alone are heavy—so the handles should be comfortable to hold with your bare hands. They should also be easy enough to hold or grip while wearing oven mitts. Large surface area A larger cooking surface relative to the total liquid volume means more space for browning meat and other ingredients with less risk of crowding, which can cause things to steam rather than brown. If you remember Julia Child's advice for making boeuf bourguignon, do not crowd the meat! A tight-fitting lid A Dutch oven’s lid should fit snugly on the pot and not rattle around when you’re carrying it or boiling water in it. That said, it’s normal for some steam to escape from even a heavy tight-fitting lid when water inside is at a rolling boil. A long warranty Enameled cast iron, in theory, is very durable, and the very best Dutch ovens are heirloom-quality pieces that will last at least a lifetime with proper care. If a manufacturer offers a very short warranty on their enameled cast-iron cookware, it could (though may not always) indicate a lower-quality product. Other Dutch ovens we liked Made In fits in the middle tier here, as it is a great Dutch oven made with a higher standard of quality than budget models. It is heavier than both Staub and Le Creuset, and the handles are divisive among staff. Some like the wide flat handles for holding when full, while others find there to be not as much knuckle clearance, making them more challenging to grasp completely with oven mitts on. This is a good Dutch oven that had a brief run as our budget pick (before Goldilocks became available), as it comes with a limited lifetime warranty not typical for budget Dutch ovens. It performs well, and was lighter than other budget Dutch ovens. The drawback is that the handles are slimmer than I'd like for easy gripping. Amazon Basics’ kitchen gear is really hit or miss, but the Amazon Basics Dutch oven is surprisingly good—especially for something with such an accessible price tag. This was also a former budget pick. Performance wise it gets the job done. Like the Zulay, it has narrow handles. It’s a good option for home cooks on a budget. However, unlike the Zulay Dutch oven, which has a lifetime warranty, this one comes with a one-year warranty, so inspect it for defects as soon as its out of the box. Overall, our testers were impressed with this sleek, stylish 5.5-quart dutch oven from DTC lifestyle brand Kana. The smooth, light interior enamel produced an even sear on both meat and vegetables, and we didn’t experience any cold spots or notice any chips in the enamel out of the box (some customer reviews have complained of chipped enamel). It’s about a pound lighter than the comparably sized Le Creuset, which means it can heat up and cool down a bit quicker, but the thinner cast iron won't retain heat quite as well. If you want a budget pot and like the modern look (or you really want a moderately priced Dutch oven with a gold-toned knob), the Milo by Kana is a good choice. Dutch ovens we don’t recommend This large, oval Dutch oven from Great Jones is gorgeous. We love the color options, and for a 6.75-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven from a popular brand, the sub-$200 price tag is nice too. But, with only one rather large size and the oval shape, it’s not the best option for everyday use—or for induction cooktops with round “burners.” But it’s the perfect size for roasting a whole chicken and large cuts of meat, and the large loop handles are easy to grab with or without oven mitts. Great Jones does offer a smaller round Dutch oven, the Dutch Baby but at 3.5 quarts it’s on the small side of the Dutch oven sweet spot. Tramontina’s relatively affordable stainless-steel cookware is often compared to All-Clad, so we had high hopes for the Brazilian brand’s 5.5-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven too. Out of the box, we liked the tall sides (great for deep-frying), but unfortunately it just didn't perform well in our testing. Our testers noticed a persistent cold spot that resulted in uneven cooking—and food sticking to the smooth, light interior enamel. We like Cuisinart’s enameled cast-iron skillet, but the Dutch oven is disappointing. Unlike the skillet, which has a dark, textured interior enamel, the Dutch oven has a smooth, light interior that didn’t perform well in our sear test. We also found multiple cold spots even when it was fully preheated, which produced pork that was unevenly cooked. In addition to its popular pottery and ceramic tableware, English brand Denby offers a small selection of enameled cast-iron cookware, including several Dutch ovens—which it calls “casseroles.” They’re moderately priced compared to similarly sized Dutch ovens from other well-known brands. When we tested the round 5.5-quart (listed as a 26-cm size) the performance was adequate, but the handles were small and hard to grab, especially when it was hot. And overall, nothing about it wowed us. But if you like the look and it’s within your budget—and you don’t mind the small handles—you may be happy with the Denby Dutch oven. We love a lot of KitchenAid gear (hello, gorgeous stand mixer!) but in general, we haven’t been that impressed with the brand’s cookware, and that trend continued with the enameled cast-iron Dutch oven didn’t impress us—though we were certainly impressed with its heft. The 6-quart Dutch oven weighs 20 pounds, empty! That’s the only size available, and it only comes in two colors too. The first time we tested Misen’s Dutch oven, we really liked it. It’s large and deep, which is great for deep-frying, and it made a pretty good stockpot too. But then Misen changed some design elements—most notably it did away with the traditional Dutch oven lid and instead offers the choice of either a silicone option or an enameled cast-iron grill pan that can double as a lid (a traditional lid is available on the larger 7-quart model, which, as we've said, is bigger than most people need). Both lid alternatives made this less functional and appealing than it was when it had a traditional enameled cast-iron lid with a metal knob. Also: Our testers have experienced some minimal enamel chipping with long-term use. This 4-quart Dutch oven from Vermicular comes as-is or alongside Vermicular’s Musui-Kamado, a stand-alone induction heating element that holds the pot, sort of like a very high-end, precise slow cooker. The interior enamel is an off-white color and minimally textured, though not as textured as the dark interior enamel of the Staub. The rim is unfinished to provide a “precision seal.” However, this makes it susceptible to rust, and during testing, did not do a better job at sealing in moisture than the Le Creuset or Staub, which do have an enamel coating around the rim. The side handles on the lid were also unnecessary, and made it difficult to grab, especially when removing it from the oven. This is one of the few cast-iron Dutch ovens we've tried without an enamel coating. While this is a beautiful piece of cookware, it’s the sort of thing that only really makes sense for dedicated cast-iron enthusiasts who love to care for and maintenance their cookware. We’ve found that developing a seasoning on this is quite challenging, and that the type of cooking we generally employ our Dutch ovens for (soups, braises, stews) tends to hinder the process. Smithey recommends a just-cook-with-it method for developing the seasoning, and the brand also claims that it’s fine to use when making soups or acidic braises. However, we found that tomato sauce stripped the seasoning and developed a metallic taste. A really robust seasoning would potentially withstand this, but you’d need to do several rounds of seasoning on your own, and with a big pot like this, that isn’t an easy task. We also found that the cast-iron lid is prone to rust spots. This is because (if you’re primarily cooking on the stovetop with your Dutch oven) the lid never gets hot enough as has no direct contact with fat, which means that it will not develop a seasoning as you cook with it. This is a problem especially because moisture condenses on the interior of the lid while cooking. All in all, having an uncoated Dutch oven is a labor of love. If you do a lot of deep-frying, or cooking on open fires, or you just really like to season cast iron as a hobby, you might be able to tame this beast. If you’re just looking for a regular-shmegular Dutch oven, we’d advise against it. Over the years, we've have tested both Lodge Essentials Dutch ovens and Lodge USA Enamel Dutch ovens, the latter of which is made in a newer manufacturing facility in North America. Unfortunately, not all Lodge cookware is created equally, and even though the USA Enamel line is clearly a much higher quality than the Lodge Essentials enameled cast iron, customers have complained about chipping with both. On the other hand, a colleague has been using a Dutch oven from the USA Enamel line for more than a year and hasn’t experienced any chipping. The issue here seems to be inconsistency in quality, but we’ll continue to use these Dutch ovens to see if the newer lines prove to be more durable. FAQ What size Dutch oven should I get? The size you get really depends on what you’ll use it for—if you’re cooking every night for a family of six, a 7-quart Dutch oven will make sense. But for most home cooks (and anyone with four or fewer people in their house), the Dutch oven sweet spot size is 5.5 or 6 quarts. It’s big enough to accommodate a pot roast or a whole chicken, but not too big for a loaf of sourdough if you’re the bread-baking type. It’s also a good size for deep-frying and gives you plenty of room for tossing four servings of pasta without overcrowding the pan. What material is a Dutch oven made of? Dutch ovens can be made of various types of metal or ceramic, and they can be enamel-coated or uncoated. For example, Emile Henry makes an enameled clay ceramic Dutch oven and Dansk makes an enameled carbon-steel Dutch oven (er, “casserole”). You can even get high-quality raw cast-iron Dutch ovens from brands like Smithey and Lancaster, but they require seasoning and more maintenance than enameled cast iron. However, its enameled cast-iron Dutch ovens that are ubiquitous. The cast iron offers incredible heat retention and is compatible with gas, electric, and induction cooktops while the durable porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion caused by water as well as acidic foods like tomatoes. The enamel also eliminates the need for seasoning. Are Dutch ovens nonstick? One of the biggest misconceptions about this kind of cookware is that the cooking surface is supposed to be nonstick. It’s not. Porcelain enamel may look like a ceramic nonstick coating, and it’s far easier to clean and care for than raw cast iron, but it is not a nonstick surface. Its purpose is to protect the cast iron underneath. That said, with the right temperature and enough butter or oil, food releases from enamel pretty easily. How do I protect my Dutch oven from damage? Enameled cast iron can withstand high heat as well as freezing temperatures, but you do want to avoid thermal shock to your Dutch oven. For example: Don’t take it from the fridge and put it straight over high heat on your stovetop. And when you’re preheating it, do it slowly over low to medium heat. Sudden temperature changes can cause the enamel to chip and in some cases damage the cast iron itself (up to and including actually cracking it), and this kind of damage will often be grounds for the manufacturer to void the warranty. Why shouldn’t I use metal utensils in my Dutch oven? Though some user manuals say metal utensils are fine in their enameled cast-iron cookware, it’s best to use wood or silicone. Metal utensils can, over time, damage the protective enamel, especially if you use them in a hot pot. Even minor, cosmetic scratch marks from metal utensils can be an issue because you may be tempted to buff them out with an abrasive cleaner. Doing that once or twice might not cause any major damage, but repeated use of abrasive cleaners will absolutely erode the top layer of the porcelain enamel and eventually make it porous and prone to much worse staining. What’s the deal with braising divots? Many Dutch oven lids are pocked with divots, which supposedly help to evenly distribute moisture when braising—in theory, kind of basting the meat inside the closed pot. That said, in many years of testing, we haven’t seen any clear evidence of this actually happening. How should I clean a Dutch oven? Enameled cast-iron cookware is incredibly durable because the porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion. And unlike traditional and ceramic nonstick cookware, a high-quality enamel coating can last forever if you take good care of it—which, sorry to say, means never putting it in the dishwasher. While it’s true that some enameled cast-iron pieces, including Le Creuset’s colorful Dutch ovens, are marketed as dishwasher-safe, if you read the manual, you’ll learn that most manufacturers generally recommend hand-washing. That’s because over time, harsh dishwasher detergents can erode the enamel, making it more porous, which can lead to staining and stuck-on food.

item.title: A New Museum, Cruise Haute Couture, and Gorgeous Glassware: Here's What's Exciting Us in Travel Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.41
Whether you're on land or at sea, in a bar or in Bahrain, there are myriad reasons for design lovers to get excited about travel right now. In the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler, we went long on a number of these stories—how Como's enduring craft traditions help make it one of the planet's most luxurious destinations, why Fort Worth is the sartorial epicenter of the rise of ranchcore in fashion. But we also collected a few juicy morsels worth sharing in brief. There's a new museum in the Middle East to earmark if you're interested in the intersection of craft and history, and a French cruise line has launched a new itinerary that will bring haute couture to the high seas. Read on for all we think you should know. A gem of a new museum on Bahrain's pearling path “Inside an elegant home formerly owned by a wealthy merchant family in Bahrain's coastal city of Muharraq sits the two-year-old Siyadi Pearl Museum. The space is the latest addition to the Pearling Path, which connects important structures from the city's pearling history. Along its two miles are 17 significant sites; public squares shaded by flame trees; and a pedestrian bridge that reconnects Muharraq with its original shoreline, which has been mostly lost to development. Terrazzo lampposts topped by pearl-shaped light bulbs double as trail markers. Tales of wealth are told in the grand living quarters of merchants and traders; those of hardship in the display of the simple tools pearl divers relied on (nose clips, stone weights, leather finger covers) during arduous months aboard dhows at sea.” —Nicola Chilton High fashion comes to the high seas “In September 2027, French line Ponant will sail a commonly traveled route along Italy's coast with an entirely unique agenda: placing the country's fashion maisons at the center of the passenger experience. Sailing down the coast from Tuscany and then up to Venice, guests on board the intimate Le Boréal will experience five major haute labels. They will chat with a Brioni tailor about making the perfect alterations; observe a master craftsperson cut precious gemstones at iconic jeweler Pomellato; and explore two historic sites in Florence tied to Gucci via the Palazzo Gucci and the 15th-century Palazzo Settimanni, home to the Gucci archives. Think of this as high fashion on the high seas.” —Erin Florio Drinks wear designer around the globe “Striking, artisanal glassware that upstages the concoction it holds is the coolest thing in cocktail culture these days. Here, bars around the world and the gorgeously unique vessels you may just encounter while there.” —Michelle Tchea This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.
