item.title: Where to Stay in Great Smoky Mountains National Park for Mountain Views and Fall Foliage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.11
Frequently named the most visited national park in the US, Great Smoky Mountains have universal appeal—travelers come from all over the country (and the world) to enjoy the natural beauty of this part of North Carolina and Tennessee. Hikers, anglers, photographers, road-trippers, birders, families, and thrill-seekers can all find reasons to make the trek. Whether you want to see the namesake fog blanketing the peaks—many of which tower well over 6,000 feet—breathe in the crisp air, or glimpse the famous wildflowers and fall foliage, there’s plenty to do, and some excellent places to spend the night once you get here. From the historic LeConte Lodge—the only lodging within the park’s boundaries—with its hard-to-come-by reservations and hike-in access to some of the South’s most luxurious hotels—Blackberry Farm and The Swag are legendary in the hospitality world—there’s something for every type of traveler. Whether it’s your first time exploring the park or you’re planning a return trip, you have options for where to set up your base camp. You can opt for a rustic cabin rental, a kid-friendly resort, or a stylish glamping site depending on your mood. Read on for some of the best places to stay near Great Smoky Mountains National Park for your next nature-filled adventure. How to plan a trip to Great Smoky Mountains National Park How do you get to Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Great Smoky Mountains National Park sits along the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. If you’re flying into the area, McGhee Tyson Airport (TYS) in Knoxville, Tennessee, and Asheville Regional Airport (AVL) are among the most convenient options. From TYS, it’s a 30- and 60-minute drive, respectively, to the park’s main entrances in Townsend and Gatlinburg, Tennessee. The drive from AVL to the entrance in Cherokee, North Carolina, will take you a little over an hour. When is the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Undoubtedly, the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park is in the fall. If you time it right—keep an eye on the foliage reports—you’ll witness the splendor of all the reds, oranges, and yellows. The changing colors typically start to appear in late September, and they peak between mid-October and mid-to-early November, depending on the weather and elevation. This time of year also tends to be the busiest season in the park, so keep that in mind when you’re planning a trip (book early and visit mid-week if possible). How long should you visit the Great Smoky Mountains? Because of the size and plethora of things to do within the park, you’ll want to plan for multiple days of exploration—I’d recommend at least three. That way, you can drive the scenic loops, complete a few hikes, and check off all the major sites without rushing. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Where Was 'The Shards' Filmed? Where ‘80s LA Nostalgia Still Exists Today
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.03
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Shards filmed? The Shards, FX’s new adaptation of American Psycho author Bret Easton Ellis’s 2023 autofiction thriller, opens with protagonist and narrator Bret (Igby Rigney) driving to the Bruin Theater in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. He buys a ticket at the booth out front and sits down to watch The Shining in 70-mm. His present-day voice-over floats in, remarking on how strange it was to see a movie in 1980, without distractions like smartphones and social media. While waiting, he glances at the ornate Art Deco ceiling, taking note of every gorgeous detail. In reality, the Bruin is now shuttered; there was never a ticket booth out front, and the ceiling featured in the show is from the Fox Theater across the street. But thanks to production designer and native Angeleno Cat Smith, Bret’s day at the cinema feels as true as memory. Memory is central to The Shards, as a fictionalized Ellis recounts how he and his elite prep school pals were targeted by a serial killer nicknamed “The Trawler” during their senior year. While Smith was thankfully never the subject of a manhunt, she did go to an LA prep school in the ‘80s, and it’s her ultra-specific memories of the time that flesh out such an authentic and believable backdrop for the show. I spoke with Smith about The Shards, the city so integral to its story, and how she went about recreating such a distinct version of it—here are some excerpts from our conversation. The Shards is so intrinsically LA that it feels like a character. When you began this process with Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis, what was the main thing they asked of you in curating the vibe of the city? I’m a local, so I know the city really well. And I also went to a private school in Los Angeles, kind of in the period just about when Bret wrote his book. So I had a really intrinsic memory of that, and we just try to get as close to the actual as we can. Ryan’s influence from the beginning was American Gigolo, and what’s great about that movie is that it was filmed in 1981. He takes walks through areas of Los Angeles that are completely authentic to the time because it wasn’t a period piece, and it’s amazing what he sees. The entire Westwood Village was there. Ryan thought of a very muted palette, grays and whites, and this is ‘81, so it’s not the height of ‘80s design, just the edge. You’re turning into the ‘80s from the late ‘70s, where you would have those browns and reds, while the ‘80s were those pastels and stronger colors that came later. So it was kind of a combination of those two distinct eras. Are there any places in the city that have stayed in that same design style as in American Gigolo? We did shoot in the Westwood Village, and the Bruin and Westwoods theaters are the same because they were built in the ‘30s. Although the theater [Bret] went into was closed temporarily, and it didn’t have a concessions booth outside, so we had to build that. But when you come outside, we were able to copy the street from Westwood at the time. When you pass by the theater and you look behind, all of those are façades we put up, but that street was mainly still the architecture of that time. There’s this beautiful shot of the ceiling of the Bruin Theater in the pilot. Why are design details like that so important in your storytelling? Right! Because that’s what you’ll find in LA, those theaters kept those details. That’s something that either we, as a city, thought was worthwhile, or they renovated it. In this particular case, it’s actually the Fox Theater interior. We cheated it. They really loved the way the Bruin looked on the outside, but the inside of the Fox was in better shape. There’s certain things that people find important, that they keep. And one of those things that they don’t keep is shopping malls. Were you guys shooting in the [Sherman Oaks] Galleria? No. The Galleria, even though it still exists under that name, is not what you would see then. They shot Fast Times at Ridgemont High there, and that’s what it would’ve looked like at that very time. I had to find something that looked like the Galleria in 1980, and there’s not a lot in Los Angeles that would give you that. I mean, the most memorable thing was this amazing skylight that covers the whole ceiling and glass elevators and escalators that go up three stories. So we went to the South Coast Plaza, and they do have all of that, but the problem is, of course, they’ve renovated it probably more than once. Now it would be a shopping experience that’s recognizable to you today: it’s all glass, the signage is either very subtle or completely crazy. And the stuff they have is so specific to today, like they have this weird virtual reality room. None of it is appropriate for the ‘80s, so we had to go there and figure out exactly what our shots were, and then redo the facades of like ten spaces. We did the movie theater, Orange Julius, Licorice Pizza, Swensen’s Ice Cream—although you never saw that one—and we did Vince’s Pets. All those existed in the Galleria. We did a Casual Corner, Judy’s, this horrible place called One Potato, Two Potato. It was so much fun. We weren’t given a huge budget, but I wanted it to recall that very strong memory I had of shopping in the Galleria and going to movies in that theater. How do you think your experiences as an LA native helped create such an authentic depiction of that time period without feeling forced? Well, I was a little bit disdainful going into this, thinking “I’m gonna show them what it was really like.” And then I realized everybody who worked on this, who had lived through it, has a different memory of what it actually was, which I think leads to more interesting design, because then you end up with layers. This person remembers this, and that person remembers that, and when you put them together, that’s what it really was. But also AI has completely corrupted people’s view of what the ‘80s was, so I had to be really careful that I wasn’t getting mesmerized by these fake images of what the ‘80s was versus an actual advertisement for a bedroom set or a picture from Architectural Digest from that year. You always see something unexpected there that you don’t see in the AI images, like weird artwork or way too many plants. You’ve got to throw it into a blender because it gets so caught up in what people’s personal tastes were, which weren’t always great. They may see something in an Architectural Digest and their version of it in their own house is not quite as tasteful as you’d want it to be. I love that. We did a lot of location scouting of houses where they kept the ‘80s design, which is crazy if you think about it. There was this street in the Valley that looked almost untouched from the ‘80s, even the signage wasn’t that bad. What do you think The Shards says about LA as a city now? It’s very insular. I always worry that when people come to LA, they’ll be very lonely. It’s hard to meet people, you have to get around by car. There’s people who already have a community who don’t allow new people to be a part of that community. But the interesting thing about LA is that there’s so many layers here, I’m never bored looking around. I’ll look around and see the craziest detail. It’s such an ambiguous place that the detail stands out, because you’re not looking in a sea of that. You’re looking at a sea of blankness when this beautiful thing appears that tells you something about life situations. And we’re living in a time that’s very similar to the 80s. I always told my son: “You shouldn’t love the 80s, it was a dark, depressing time.” There were a lot of drugs, a lot of gun violence, everybody was out for themselves. The rich were kings. Sound familiar? And then I left him this world that was identical.

item.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.03
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions was something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveler, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’sfilming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: Decoding Ho Chi Minh City's Vibrant Fashion Scene
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.79
A mosaic of skyscrapers, colonial mansions, and aging shophouses, Qun 1—or District 1—forms the heart of Ho Chi Minh City, still referred to by its former name, Saigon. Once the cultural and administrative hub of French Indochina, the area has evolved into Saigon's luxury corridor, where international boutiques, art galleries, Michelin-starred restaurants, and some of the city's most expensive retail real estate now cluster within a few dense, walkable blocks. In the last decade District 1 has also become the clearest stage for Vietnam's fashion transformation. For years the country was known globally as a manufacturing powerhouse, producing garments for brands like Nike and Calvin Klein, but few outside the region could name a Vietnamese designer. That has changed. A new generation of labels—drawing from Saigon street culture, contemporary art, and heritage textiles—has repositioned Vietnam from production base to cultural exporter. That shift is increasingly visible with domestic brands like Latui Atelier and Lsoul appearing on such celebrities as Katy Perry and Blackpink's Jennie, while Ho Chi Minh City itself has emerged as a shopping destination for international travelers. Fueling this renaissance is the country's youthful optimism: Vietnam is one of the world's fastest-growing economies, and more than half its population is under 35. A new era of creatives and consumers is forging a fashion identity that is distinctly Vietnamese yet globally minded. Along streets like Đng Khi and Lê Li, locals and clued-in tourists hunt homegrown labels in stores once dominated by Western brands. From youth-driven collectives to refined tailoring studios, here's a curated guide to shopping in District 1. The multibrand retailers The new luxury anchor of the scene, Rue Miche is often compared to Dover Street Market for its gallery-like staging of local talent. The original boutique on Phùng Kh c Khoan street was joined in late 2025 by Rue Miche L'Édition, a roughly 50,000-square-foot flagship in the basement of the sprawling Union Square mixed-use complex. Since opening, the store has amassed nearly 90 Vietnamese labels across both locations; standouts include Americana-inspired Aah Midnight Club and Latui Atelier, known for shredded denim and provocative cuts. Built on a philosophy its founders sum up as “beautiful fashion and beautiful people,” the fast-growing, sustainability-minded concept store Compound Garment now houses 22 local brands within two adjacent shophouses on Nguyn Công Tr. Showcasing labels that share a visual language of oversized silhouettes, gender-fluid styling, and streetwear-inflected design, it's the most reliable read on what young Saigonese are wearing. The OG of multiconcept retailers in Vietnam since 2017, the New Playground boasts 70-plus Vietnamese labels, including Hades and Dirty Coins, across two District 1 locations (plus one in Hanoi). The original 26 Lý T Trng mainstay, with 40-plus stores, feels like a street market crossed with a concept mall kitted out in industrial mesh, neon, and Gen Z energy. The indie standouts At Gia Studios, fourth-generation tailor Lâm Gia Khang, a Project Runway Vietnam alum, translates regional craftsmanship into globally fluent looks. Traditional materials like Lãnh Mỹ A, a black dyed silk, appear in sharply modern cuts: double-breasted blazers, flowy trousers, and draped skirts. Now stocked at Lane Crawford and Ssense—and recently worn by Zoe Saldaña and Emma Stone—it's among Vietnam's most internationally recognized labels. Gia means “home” or “family”; fittingly, the designer's mother oversees production. On the more experimental end, Parsons-trained designer Tom Trandt's Môi Điên (literally, “crazy lips”; figuratively, “outspoken”) has built a cult following around pleating, sculptural minimalism, and gender-fluid silhouettes that feel both futuristic and traditional. Since launching a decade ago, the label has mined Vietnamese folk imagery, street culture, and dead stock textiles for its collections. Rather than treating the men's traditional áo dài as ceremonial dress, photographer-artist Thiên Minh's Mêman reframes it for everyday life. The label works primarily in Japanese linen and neutral palettes, producing collections that reinterpret Vietnamese heritage through a practical minimalist lens. New-school rebels Keep Fashion Weird is the motto of Duc Studio, whose voluminous, deconstructed pieces evoke a sense of daring. Think full-print riffs on Vietnam's national dress, the áo dài, and handcrafted denim and layered silhouettes. Designer Nguyn Minh Đc started the label in 2019 and entered ready-to-wear in 2021. A puffy bag of his was later spotted on Bella Hadid; more recent pieces have been worn by astronaut and activist Amanda Nguyen and the Vietnamese rapper Hieuthuhai. Nguyn Trng Lâm's Lsoul focuses on hyperfeminine glam: corsetry, lace, and shapes that seem engineered for svelte pop stars. To wit, the members of the pop group Blackpink and singer Madison Beer have all worn the brand, which also recently debuted a runway collection at Shanghai Fashion Week. The label Victim of the Prime launched at a small District 1 boutique in 2022; two years later it opened a larger flagship store right around the corner. The gender-neutral aesthetic is clean, youthful, and slightly cerebral—the brand's slogan is We're All Victims of Something Bigger Than Us. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: The Best Fall Foliage in the USA: A Guide to Where to Go This Autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
It’s a rare occasion that vast swaths of the United States experience a season in a similar way—but the sepia-toned mosaic of fall foliage soon to sprawl across the country in a few short weeks proves that fall is the one exception to that rule. Starting as early as late September and extending well into November, you can expect to find some combination of red, gold, yellow, and orange bathing the trees from coast to coast. But anyone well-versed in leaf-peeping—or the colloquial nickname given to any tourist with a proclivity for fall foliage gazing—knows that some states and regions have more colorful and sweeping offerings than others. So for any looking to leaf-peep-maxx this upcoming fall, we took the liberty of rounding up the states, parks, and areas from across the country where you can expect to find the most vibrant fall tableaus come this October. Blue Ridge Mountains, North Georgia Way down on the south of the eastern shore you’ll find a range of mountains absolutely awash for fall. The Blue Ridge Mountain region of North Georgia makes up a smaller enclave of the greater Appalachian Mountains—and though you can’t go wrong with any stop along the Appalachian Trail when it comes to fall foliage, this little corner right on the border between Georgia and Tennessee is especially ideal for the changing seasons. The Southern climate makes things a little milder, without having to sacrifice the fall grandeur. The area skews more towards nature aficionados, with plenty of nature paths and mountain trails to climb. One particular favorite includes Brasstown Bald, where you can catch the best view of the leaves in peak color. Where to stay in the Blue Ridge Mountains: - A charming Victorian B&B: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast - A peaceful mountain escape: The Copperhead Lodge The Berkshires, Massachusetts When it comes to the idyllic pastoral regions of New England, Massachusetts’s Berkshires are right up there with the likes of New York's Adirondacks. One look around and you can see exactly how the lush area inspired writers like Edith Wharton and artists like Norman Rockwell (and if you don’t, just take a quick trip to the Norman Rockwell Museum). Other highlights for our Berkshires guide includes shopping at stores like Fluff Alpaca, hiking up Monument Mountain’s three different trails, grabbing some coffee beans from West Stockbridge’s famous No. Six Depot, and ordering a bite off the farm-to-table menu at Prairie Whale. Pair all of that with the area’s bustling boutique hotel scene in Lenox, Massachusetts, and you’ve got one must-see stop on your Great American leaf-peeping tour. Where to stay in the Berkshires: - For an artistic flair: 33 Main - A motor-lodge-turned luxury hotel: Life House Stowe, Vermont Nestled in the embrace of Vermont’s Green Mountains, Stowe might be known for its slopes and skiing—but it’s also one of the best places to catch a verifiable sea of fall foliage come October and November. This is your quintessential idyllic northern New England escape. While it’s had its fair share of development, there are plenty of locals who reside in the town year-round. Pre-game leaf-peeping by exploring the microbrewing scene or shopping for some top-of-the-line maple products at Shaw’s General Store. It’s also something of a hikers paradise, with absolutely no small shortage of trails for the ambitious explorers and gentler strollers alike. No matter what you choose, there’s sure to be one fantastic view. Where to stay in Stowe, Vermont: - For a hygge vibe: Field Guide - A spa-retreat: AWOL Stowe - A traditionally intimate ski lodge: Edson Hill Great Smoky Mountains, Tennessee and North Carolina The Great Smoky Mountains that trail up the border between Tennessee and North Carolina earned their name from the natural, gauzy fog that often drapes across the region. It gives the area an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality during any time of year. Add in a mosaic of fall foliage and it's no wonder why this spot is home to some of the best fall foliage in the USA. See the sights from the famous Cades Cove loop or hike the Laurel Falls Trail or any of the many paths along the mountains. You’ll also find a range of different lodging options in the area—including glamping experiences, cabins, farms, and more. Where to stay in the Great Smoky Mountains: - An irreverent farm getaway: Blackberry Farm - A sprawling ranch: Cataloochee Ranch - A one-of-a-kind glamping stay: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains Aspen, Colorado Aspen is one of those cold weather destinations that’s spoken of with an undeniable air of prestige—the same way you would speak of Lake Como in the spring, or the French Riviera in summer. Like Stowe, it’s most famous for its skiing, but it’s got its fair share of foliage to show off around fall. Especially ideal for those who have a taste for the finer things in life, Aspen’s also a prime luxury shopping destination. Shop high end designer brands like Prada or Gucci, and grab a chic cowboy hat from Kemo Sabe. And you can’t forget the decadent fare available at eateries like Bosq, White House Tavern, Matsushia, and more. Where to stay in Aspen, Colorado: - An Aspen mainstay: Hotel Jerome Sun Valley, Idaho Another skiing staple, Sun Valley has long charmed celebrities and nature-lovers alike. It’s renowned for its skiing but offers golden escape during the shoulder season of fall. Sun Valley’s especially great for any leaf peepers who happen to also be fans of Ernest Hemingway. The famous Lost Generation author loved the region and even finished his book For Whom The Bell Tolls in the Sun Valley Resort’s suite 206. Hemingway’s admiration of and attachment to the area is immortalized with with a memorial and free audio walking tour. Where to stay in Sun Valley, Idaho: - A historic ski resort: Sun Valley Resort - For a laidback lodging: Limelight Ketchum North Cascades, Washington New England often takes the cake when it comes to fall foliage, but don’t write off the Pacific Northwest. One drive along the Cascade Loop will show that this craggy region has its own verdancy amid the snow dusted mountains. Often referred to as the American Alps, there are plenty of peaks and summits to see the leaves—such as the Washington Pass overlooking the Liberty Bell Mountain—while hiking trails like the Maple Pass Loop and Blue Lake offer some of the best opportunities for leaf-peeping. Where to stay in North Cascades, Washington: - A floating cabin: Ross Lake Resort Laurel Hill, Pennsylvania There are plenty of trails and state parks you can take advantage of to gaze at the Pennsylvania foliage. There’s Mount Davis, Ohiopyle State Park, Laurel Hill state park, and so much more. You really can’t go wrong with any of them. But we’d recommend conducting your leaf peeping from inside, specifically inside one of famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s most well-known works. Dubbed Fallingwater, this quintessentially mid-century modern structure sits atop a waterfall and is entirely ensconced in a forest of trees—making its airy interiors the ideal framing for the lush colors of fall. Where to stay in Laurel Highlands Pennsylvania: - A sprawling estate: Nemacolin Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire Rounding off the New England stops, this nature reserve is nestled in the middle of New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest. Here, you’ll find parts of the larger Appalachian Trail, as well as hikes up well-known peaks like Artist Bluff—which afford panoramic views of the area’s famous Echo Lake. The body of water sits at the base of Cannon Mountain and perfectly reflects the prism of color around it, even more so when those colors are the rich reds, golds, yellows, and oranges of fall. Where to stay in Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire: - A mansion inn: The Franconia Inn Adirondacks, New York You just need to watch one episode of Gilmore Girls to know that New England is one of the top best places to see fall foliage, and the Adirondacks is one of the region’s best fall exports. Located just about four hours outside of New York City, this mountain area encompasses much of New York’s storied “upstate” region—where people escape from the city to ensconce themselves in the privacy of cozy cabins, lake houses, and more. Here, you’ll find over 3,000 lakes and ponds—such as the famous Lake Placid—and the Adirondack High Peaks. Grab a quick drink at Raquette River Brewing or fill up on French-Canadian comfort dishes at Woodshed on Park, before heading out to take in the vivid leaves. Where to stay in the Adirondacks: - For a luxurious lake island resort: The Sagamore Resort - A rustic log cabin experience: The Point - A Lake Placid classic: Great Adirondack Hotel Columbia River Gorge, Northern Oregon Just above California and below other fall foliage fave Washington, the Northern Oregon region similarly offers plenty of mystically foggy places to peep some leaves. What’s even better is you get the best of both worlds with forests and beaches colliding to make up this scenic coast. Travel through the Columbia River Gorge to see all the leaves, then take a road trip out to Cannon Beach to top the adventure off. Where to stay in Northern Oregon: - A water-front property: Cannery Pier Hotel & Spa Shenandoah National Park, Virginia Just off the Blue Ridge Parkway, and not too far from the border of West Virginia, Shenandoah National Park extends about 197,439 acres across Virginia’s Blue Ridge region. It’s got breathtaking views and nature, making it ideal to catch some of the best fall foliage in the USA. After all, there's a reason we named it one of the best national parks to enjoy during the fall. Shenandoah is mostly visited for hiking, with over 500 miles of trails—many of which you can find along the area’s Skyline Drive—that offer ample opportunity to take in nature, no matter the time of year.

item.title: The Distinctly Brazilian Flavor of São Paolo's Japanese Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.31
At Aizomê, a stylish Japanese restaurant shrouded by a thick wall of trees just off São Paulo’s main thoroughfare, Avenida Paulista, the food is both recognizable to devotees of Japanese cuisine and distinctly Brazilian. You might find pirarucu, an enormous Amazonian riverfish, in saikyo yaki, a traditional Japanese sweet-miso preparation more commonly used on black cod. Ponzu incorporates tucupi, a tart yellow sauce made from fermented wild manioc, a root native to the Amazon. “I’m third generation,” says owner Telma Shiraishi, who was born and raised in São Paulo and whose grandparents hail from the Wakayama and Iwate prefectures of Japan. “It doesn’t make sense for me to make a cuisine that is 100% Japanese, bringing 100% of ingredients from Japan.” Over the past 20 years of leading Aizomê, Shiraishi has been on a journey to determine how these two cultures come together in one place. What began as an effort toward a fiercely traditional Japanese eatery has evolved into a cuisine that better reflects her own experience, which she calls Nipo-Brazilian, blending Japanese and Brazilian techniques, influences, and ingredients. Of Brazil’s 214 million people, an estimated 2 million people are of Japanese descent, making it the largest community outside of Japan. The vast majority live in São Paulo. It’s a history that reaches back to 1907, when the two countries signed an agreement permitting Japanese migration to meet labor needs on coffee plantations in the southern Brazilian states of São Paulo and Paraná. Eventually those immigrants founded agricultural settlements or moved into major cities. The São Paolo neighborhood of Liberdade, often referred to as the city’s Japantown, has been the nucleus of the Japanese Brazilian community since then. When the first Japanese restaurants emerged, they largely catered to members of their own community. For decades, Japanese cuisine faced stereotyping and suspicion—Brazilians were highly wary of raw fish—but later American imports like huge sushi boats, or rolls that included cream cheese, widened the appeal. For Shiraishi, these restaurants “helped break down prejudices” and accustomed palates to the likes of soy sauce and raw fish. Now even that era feels like the past: South America’s largest city has grown to contain a kaleidoscope of options when it comes to Japanese restaurants. There is high-end omakase and kaiseki, a raft of izakayas, specialist ramen, udon, tempura, and tonkatsu joints. The scene has hugely diversified, including both truer interpretations of original dishes and a marriage of Brazilian flavors that builds on, rather than flattens, Japanese roots. There are currently 3,000 Japanese restaurants across São Paulo, and they aren’t confined to Liberdade either; they stretch throughout the city, allowing the former enclave to take on a pan-Asian personality. Shiraishi’s Nipo-Brazilian approach isn’t new, but speaks to the way that Japanese immigrants, since they first arrived in the early 20th century, needed to adapt to local ingredients: Papaya root instead of burdock; water hyacinth stalks replacing lotus roots. Shiraishi recalls her grandmother making sushi with chard leaves, which are far more plentiful in Brazil, instead of seaweed. Unlike the Philadelphia rolls and all-you-can-eat buffets, which Shiraishi felt “didn’t have any connection…to what I grew up eating,” the items now on her menu are reminiscent of the food she was raised on. This spirit lives on in Aizomé’s multicourse tasting menu, and Shiraishi continues to scour the country for ingredients that highlight the history and evolution of Japanese food in Brazil. Guests might eat chayote marinated in cachaça, a Brazilian spirit, and soy sauce. Mapará, another Amazonian fish, often replaces eel. Her dashi uses dried Brazilian fish rather than katsuobushi, and when possible, local wild mushrooms over shiitake. “The only ingredient [which] we don’t have something similar in Brazil is kombu,” says Shiraishi, referring to the umami-rich sea kelp used in much of Japanese cuisine. A rising interest in Japanese food beyond sushi has fueled another distinctly Brazilian boom: izakayas. While these casual pubs have existed in the city for decades, it's only in the past 10 years that they have become some of the city’s most popular hangouts. Izakaya Matsu, an excellent bar in Pinheiros, is perennially packed. In Liberdade, Izakaya Issa and Kintaro have thrived since the 1990s. Wagner Higuchi runs the latter, a tiny bustling bar that his parents founded in 1993. On a warm, breezy evening, the kind where paulistanos like to spill out onto the streets with ice-cold beers, patrons at Kintaro squeeze side-by-side, drinking Japanese beers and shochu with Yakult, while tucking into an array of dishes served in small aluminium containers. The food, says Higuchi, is a mix of traditional—think braised burdock root and carrot, a side dish that dates back to the Edo period—and those from the “colony,” which is how Japanese Brazilians refer to the agricultural settlements of the early 20th century, when the Japanese first settled and adapted to local ingredients, such as a vinegary marinated tilapia. Higuchi took over from his parents in 2018 and now runs the bar; his aunt and nephew man the kitchen. “We focus on homemade Japanese food,” says Higuchi. “We evoke the fond memories of our Japanese descendants, the famous ‘batchan’ [grandma] food. It’s important to maintain these traditions because the flavor of this food is unique.” Higuchi adds that a Japanese person visiting from Japan might find some of the dishes unusual, “but for a descendant who remembers the food from home and batchan’s cooking, it can bring back wonderful memories.” On the northern edge of Avenida Paulista, the elegant, minimalist Kanoê represents another recent shift: toward classic Japanese fine dining. In 2024, the Michelin Guide returned to São Paulo, and a number of Japanese spots, including Kan Suke, Kazuo, Kuro, and Kanoê, were awarded a star. Many are run by Brazilian-born chefs of Japanese heritage who spent time in Japan in an effort to master the art of sushi. Kanoê is an exclusive omakase, packed each night despite its hefty price tag—the tasting menu costs $268. Inside, though, chefs expertly slice the finest fish—from Brazil, Japan, and beyond—and serenely cook over induction stovetops. Most revered is the rice, whose provenance is a closely guarded secret and whose result is deeply vinegary and warm enough to melt the most delicate tuna imaginable. On a buzzy Saturday night, sitting across the counter from several supremely confident and concentrated chefs, the pairing of rice, Spanish bluefin tuna, and Niigata salt is arguably the greatest mouthful of sushi in the city—the kind that makes strangers turn and smile to tables beside them. São Paulo–born owner Tadashi Shiraishi (no relation to Telma) spent years cooking in Japan, Europe, and the US, honing his craft to become one of Brazil’s great sushi chefs. Though deeply rooted in Japanese tradition, he likes to break rules. Tuna is served first because most guests are too full to enjoy the fatty fish at the end of an omakase. It’s a masterstroke, highlighting the fish’s richness before more delicate scallops and hamachi. These types of high-end Japanese restaurants have emerged, in part, thanks to an increasingly wealthy and well-traveled Brazilian populace, says Tadashi, allowing São Paulo’s sushi scene to compete with the world’s gastronomic capitals, like New York. “São Paulo is one of my favorite places to eat Japanese food," he adds. Though Tadashi uses some Brazilian-grown ingredients, his restaurant has never been explicitly focused on creating Japanese Brazilian cuisine. Rather, he explains, it has always been about studying and preserving aspects of traditional Japanese cooking to share with a Brazilian audience. “The restaurant aims to operate within principles closely linked to Japanese tradition, respecting technique, seasonality, hospitality, and the creation of flavor within this framework.” Food among diasporas, perhaps inevitably, can veer further from its origins as people adapt to new countries and cultures intertwine. As with Indian food in the UK or Mexican cuisine in the US, Japanese food in São Paulo is today defined by a multitude of interpretations. There are, Tadashi says, “formats more adapted to Brazilian tastes [and] those closer to traditions and techniques originally developed in Japan, but with a more personal touch.” Indeed, Japanese cuisine in Brazil has never been more popular or varied, from the experimental to the fiercely traditional. There are temakerias in gas stations, beach kiosks selling sushi, and, still, all-you-can-eat sushi rodízios in every town. “The new generation, they don’t want to eat McDonald’s, they want sushi,” says Telma, referring to the ongoing—and yet, in this case, usurped—Brazilian adoration for international chains. This year Telma will open a new spot in Saúde, a neighborhood in the city’s south that is now home to one of the largest Japanese Brazilian communities. “As a community of descendants, we have to tell our story.” Thanks to the continued efforts of São Paulo’s vast array of Japanese Brazilian chefs, the options are better—and the story told louder—than ever before.

item.title: The Best Beaches in Miami, From Nature Reserves to Sceney Beach Clubs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.97
Miami has always known how to turn a day at the beach into a scene. This rings especially true along the sandy patches belonging to Miami Beach’s top hotels, which have been upping the stakes with cushy amenities and experiences designed to warrant hefty membership fees for locals—and generate enough revenue to keep their beach clubs at the top of their game. The good news for travelers? Book a room at such hotels—think CNT Triple Crown Winners 1 Hotel South Beach and Faena Miami Beach or the new and improved Delano Miami Beach—and many of those same privileges typically extend to hotel guests, no membership required (though nightly rates will cost ya!). Of course, you don’t need a hotel key, annual dues, or an impending inheritance to experience Miami’s best beaches. Miles of public shoreline remain gloriously democratic, whether you want to join the beautiful bodies and colorful lifeguard stands of South Beach, bike beneath the palms of Key Biscayne, kayak through mangroves at Oleta River State Park, or ditch your swimsuit altogether at liberating, clothing-optional Haulover Beach. Consider these 18 picks less a ranking of sand and more a guide to Miami’s many ways of doing the beach, popular year-round thanks to a balmy climate that makes summer feel seemingly endless. item.title: 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs for Pacific Sunsets, Storm Chasing, and Eclectic Beach Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.49
There are few places in the United States as breathtaking as the Oregon Coast, where towering spruce trees make way for vast blue horizons at what feels like the edge of the Earth. An exquisite marriage of colors, the Beaver State’s famous shoreline stretches from the Columbia River in the north to the California border in the south, lending itself to a misty, nature-filled getaway. Whether you’re interested in exploring the tide pools and gazing at the hordes of seabirds that congregate around Cannon Beach’s Haystack Rock, or staring down Thor’s Well (otherwise known as the “Drainpipe of the Pacific”) over in Yachats, these 15 Oregon Coast Airbnbs offer cozy respites for all kinds of outdoor excursions. Some are vacation spots in and of themselves, with amenities like cedar hot tubs and barrel saunas; others’ main focus is the dreamy ocean views. From A-frame cabins and tiny floating homes to glass-walled lookouts and lighthouse-shaped properties, these are the best Airbnbs for an unforgettable Pacific Northwest escape. Our top picks: - Best for solo travelers: Tiny home on Tillamook Bay - Best for views: Nehalem home five minutes from the beach - Best for families: Cabin with views of Twin Rocks - Best for beach access: Arch Cape home with a sauna and hot tub FAQ: Which Oregon Coast vacation rentals offer the best views? For truly cinematic views, Manzanita’s hillside homes provide a sweeping overlook of seven-mile Neahkahnie Beach. For quieter vistas, Oceanside and Yachats deliver raw, less-developed coastal scenery with panoramic reach. How do I get to the Oregon Coast? Most travelers begin in Portland, Oregon, which is served by Portland International Airport. From there, a rental car is essential—there’s no comprehensive train or bus network along the coast. The northern coast (Cannon Beach, Manzanita, Seaside) is about a 1 hour and 30 minute drive west via Highway 26. The central coast (Lincoln City, Depoe Bay, Newport) is reached via Highway 18 or 20 in around two to three hours. Highway 101, the coastal route, winds southward all the way to California—ideal for a slow, scenic drive with stops along the way. Be prepared for occasional fog, winding roads, and in remote stretches, limited cell service. When is the best time to visit the Oregon Coast? The Oregon Coast has no high season in the traditional sense—each season offers a distinct atmosphere. Its summer season (July to September) brings the most sun and mild warmth, perfect for beach walks, kayaking, and long coastal hikes—but also the most visitors. Fall (October to early November) is quieter, with crisp mornings, fiery foliage inland, and excellent conditions for storm-free trail adventures. Winter (late November through February) invites travelers seeking solitude and drama—this is storm-watching season, when towering waves crash under moody skies, best enjoyed from a fireside perch. Spring (March to May) is fresh and green, with fewer crowds, migrating gray whales, and tide pools alive with seasonal marine life. item.title: Vancouver’s Best Family-Friendly Hotels, From a Local Who Has Tried Them All
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.37
As someone who was born and raised in Vancouver, I’ve seen the city through all stages of life: as a curious teen looking for adventure, as a single twenty-something eager for fun, as a new mom searching for ways to entertain my toddlers, and now as a mom of teens, helping them find new thrills in the city we call home. Regardless of which stage of life you're in, Vancity has something for everyone. When I think of the best family-friendly hotels in Vancouver, I think of spots that make it easy to get around (even without a car) and that have room service or a restaurant with options for picky eaters. With three kids, I also always appreciate some extra space for everyone to settle down after a busy day of exploring. And if there’s a pool, my kids’ trip is pretty much made. For teens, the ability to roam freely on their own is another big perk, so I like a hotel that’s close to the action, with plenty to explore within walking distance. The family-friendly hotels below put you in the heart of Vancouver, with plenty of kid-friendly perks that make it easy to settle in—and hard to leave. FAQ: Where should a family stay in Vancouver? For families, downtown Vancouver is one of the most convenient places to stay, especially around Coal Harbour. You’ll be within walking distance of restaurants, shopping, and major attractions like the Vancouver Art Gallery and the Vancouver Aquarium, with the waterfront and Stanley Park just steps away. Is Vancouver worth visiting with kids? Absolutely. Vancouver packs a lot of family-friendly fun into a relatively compact city, from beaches and bike rides to aquariums and museums. Choose your hotel wisely, and you can walk, bike, or take public transit between many of the city’s top spots. Where should you take kids in Vancouver? Make the most of Vancouver’s mix of nature, culture, and city life, whatever the season. Start in Stanley Park, Canada’s largest urban park, where you can bike or walk the seawall, stop at the Vancouver Aquarium, and cool off with a dip at one of the park’s sandy beaches. Then head to Granville Island for lunch at the Public Market, followed by some shopping and playtime at the Kids Market. For a dose of culture, head to the Museum of Anthropology, where kids can get up close to towering carved poles while learning about the Indigenous cultures and stories of the region. How we choose the best hotels in Vancouver Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: The World’s Most Beautiful Libraries Worth Traveling For
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.10
The most beautiful libraries have long been more than places to check out books, though some make a particularly compelling case for lingering. As a demand for third places to gather outside of home or work continues to grow, libraries are having a moment as prime spots for idling, browsing, and simply taking a break from the bustle beyond of their opulent doors. Libraries have taken on an array of forms around the world, as reading rooms that have been tucked into former monasteries, designed as futuristic cultural hubs, and constructed in the heart of the California redwoods. While the books are still the main attraction, it certainly doesn’t hurt to be surrounded by ornate frescoes or unexpected nooks that make you want to stay a while longer. From Colombia to Qatar, these 11 libraries are worth building into your next trip, whether you are architecture-obsessed or longing to sit down in a picturesque setting with a new read. item.title: The 17 Most Beautiful National Parks in the World, From Yellowstone to the Serengeti
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.08
Some places are beautiful for one specific reason: a beach at sunset, a mountain perfectly reflected in a lake, a rainforest humming with wildlife. But national parks offer something broader. By definition, they protect entire landscapes and ecosystems—drawing a line around expanses we’ve collectively decided are too precious to lose. For travelers, having a list of designated wonders is also an easy way to know exactly where (and how) to see some of the world’s most incredible forces of nature. That could mean rafting under waterfalls in Argentina, ballooning over fairy chimneys in Türkiye, ice caving in Iceland, or hiking for three days to reach a wildflower-filled valley in India. There are many thousands of national parks around the world, so the trickiest part is narrowing down the list—but these 17, spanning six continents and encompassing an extraordinary range of scenery, are a good place to start. Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil At first glance, Lençóis Maranhenses looks like an enormous white desert—but this vast expanse contains multitudes. The park’s sand dunes are striped with turquoise and emerald lagoons (which accumulate during the rainy season), creating the effect of infinitely repeating oases. Book a five-hour bus ride from São Luís for a surreal swim break. Iguazú National Park, Argentina This park protects the Argentine side of the enormous Iguazú Falls (Iguaçu National Park is a hop over the border in Brazil), a system of some 275 roaring cascades deep in the rainforest. The bombastically—but fittingly—named Devil’s Throat is the standout waterfall here. Admire it from one of the walkways, or ride a speedboat right into the spray. Cabo Pulmo National Park, Mexico Who says national parks have to be in the mountains—or even on land at all? Located on the tip of Mexico’s Baja California Sur peninsula, Cabo Pulmo is a coastal wonderland of quiet beaches and rock formations—but its true appeal lies under the surface. Just offshore, the brilliant Pacific waters protect a vast coral reef system teeming with sea turtles and swirling schools of zooming jacks. Yellowstone National Park, United States Choosing just one US park is a near-impossible task, but Yellowstone takes the narrow lead. Not only was it the first designated national park in the country (and, by most accounts, the entire world), but its geological diversity can’t be beat—within its 2.2 million acres, you’ll find mountains, canyons, geysers, rainbow-gradient hot springs, and more. Banff National Park, Canada This one’s no surprise. Banff National Park is one of Canada’s shining stars, beloved for its staggering views of the Rockies and glacial, almost impossibly blue lakes. Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and Lake Minnewanka are all standouts, equally lovely when reflecting sunshine in summer and frozen over in winter. Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia Namib-Naukluft is the Namibia you came for: burnt-orange sand dunes, blindingly white salt pans, and the eerie skeleton trees of Deadvlei. It’s a little bit Mars, a little bit Fury Road, but an absolute original that has no peer. Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, Madagascar Madagascar is one of the world’s hardest-to-reach countries, which makes its landscapes feel even more immaculate. Case in point: the Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park. Famous for its forest of limestone needles jutting into the sky, the park is almost terrifying in its beauty—though lightened by the fact that the Malagasy word “tsingy” roughly translates to “where one cannot walk barefoot.” Noted! Serengeti National Park, Tanzania The Serengeti occupies an almost mythical space in our collective mind. The Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest move across the plains, is one of Earth’s greatest natural shows. But even in stillness, the region is magnificent—golden grasslands rolling beneath the open sky, with acacia trees punctuating the otherwise endless horizon. Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland Iceland is known as the land of fire and ice, and no place better encapsulates that dramatic epithet than Vatnajökull National Park. Its eponymous glacier and accompanying ice caves dominate the scene, but active volcanoes simmer beneath the freeze, and rivers of meltwater cut through the terrain. It’s a true study in contrasts, both elemental and chromatic—brilliant blue ice, inky black rocks. Las Salinas de Torrevieja National Park, Spain Yes, it really is that pink. Torrevieja’s salt lagoon gets its hue from microorganisms that release red pigments in saline conditions—an imperceptible process that yields magnificent results. It’s an Instagram darling, sure, but it’s also a place to appreciate nature’s inner workings and see the world through bubblegum-colored glasses. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia Plitvice Lakes National Park may not be hidden, but it sure is a gem. Sixteen interconnected lakes cascade through the forest, linked by a series of waterfalls and natural travertine barriers, and ranging in hue from brilliant turquoise to deep blue and green. Make your way through the selfie-snapping crowds, find an empty spot on one of the wooden walkways, and just stand in awe. Valley of Flowers National Park, India The name pretty much says it all: During the summer blooming season, Uttarakhand’s Valley of Flowers transforms into a huge natural garden, with wildflowers blanketing the alpine meadows in a riot of color. Getting here requires a lengthy trek (we’re talking several days) through the Himalayas, but the effort just makes the visual payoff that much sweeter. Göreme National Park, Türkiye Göreme is defined by Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, which are about as magical as they sound. The mushroom-shaped rock structures, carved over millennia by volcanic activity and erosion, are best viewed from above—namely in the basket of a hot-air balloon. Set your alarm and time your ride to sunrise, so you can be the first to watch the landscapes awaken for the day. Kelimutu National Park, Indonesia Three lakes, three wildly different colors. Kelimutu National Park’s bodies of water shift at the whims of the minerals and gases beneath the craters, so you never know exactly what shade you’ll see when you arrive—red, blue, green, or black. It’s as if Mother Nature is wearing a trio of mood rings. Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, China Located in China’s Wulingyuan Scenic Area, Zhangjiajie boasts thousands of jagged sandstone peaks that rise dramatically over lush treetops—and when mist shrouds the valley below, they almost seem to float above the clouds. (Look familiar? The park famously inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in Avatar.) Fiordland National Park, New Zealand Fiordland National Park showcases some of New Zealand’s most striking features, all in one space: mountains, rainforests, waterfalls, and deep glacial fjords. Many visitors zero in on Milford Sound, the undeniable star attraction; but there truly are no bad views here. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Australia Few landmarks are as recognizable as Uluṟu, a sandstone monolith rising from an otherwise flat and open desert. The rockface changes color depending on the sun’s position—ochre during the day, blazing orange and pink at sunset, and purple at twilight.

item.title: The Most Beautiful Italian Coastal Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.01
Most first-time visitors to Italy tend to concentrate on cities like Rome, Florence, and Venice, but if you ask us, off-the-beaten-path Italian coastal towns are some of the most beautiful places in the country. After all, Italy has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, and some of the country’s coastal settlements predate the Roman Empire. From Liguria all the way down to Calabria, not to mention the Adriatic Coast and the islands, there are charming seaside villages that offer a wide variety of experiences. You might want the glamour of world-famous resort towns like Portofino, Capri, and Taormina, where your dolce vita fantasies can come to life. Or perhaps you’d prefer more under-the-radar towns like Maratea and Carloforte, where you can get an authentic taste of local life. In Italy, most coastal towns come alive in the summer, when visitors from around the world hit the beaches. If you want to avoid the crowds, plan to visit coastal towns in the off-season, but keep in mind that some of them all but shut down in the winter. Spring and fall are usually a good compromise. Read on to learn about 25 of the best Italian coastal towns, with Condé Nast Traveler-approved recommendations of where to stay. item.title: Should You Travel to Nepal Right Now? What Locals Want International Travelers to Know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.54
I arrive in Kathmandu on the last day of August, just five days after devastating flash floods—caused by a glacier and rock collapse along Nepal’s border with China—swept through the Rasuwa district. Entire villages and communities were wiped out, hundreds killed, and thousands more are still missing, including many tourists. It’s an unthinkable tragedy that has unfolded with devastating consequences across parts of Nepal and neighboring Tibet. As I exit baggage claim at Tribhuvan International Airport, one of a tiny handful of non-Nepalis on my flight from Dubai, I see a Flood Related Information & Help Desk manned by police. Outside the airport, the streets are busy, a cacophony of honking horns and motorbikes buzzing between cars, buses, and tuk-tuks as people travel around the Nepalese capital. Here, at least on the surface, things seem normal. I’m welcomed at The Dwarika’s hotel by René Vijay Shrestha Einhaus, owner and CEO of Dwarika’s Collection. After a warm hello, the floods are the first thing we speak of; they’re in the minds and heavy hearts of everyone here. It’s a grave catastrophe that has shaken the nation. But what’s also in the minds of Nepalis is the concern that travelers to the tourism-dependent country, about to come into its peak travel season, will stop visiting. Drinking tea in the courtyard of The Dwarika’s hotel, surrounded by centuries-old Newari wood carvings, the twittering of sparrows, and the chattering of mynahs coming home to roost, feels surreally calm. As we chat, monsoon rains start pouring from the sky, a constant, thunderous downpour that hammers on the rooftops and trees, only letting up in the early hours of the following morning. It doesn’t bode well for those in the areas directly affected by the floods, or for those trying to help them. Look at a map of Nepal and the devastated areas don’t appear all that far from the capital, but the country’s mountainous topography means that there’s no direct route between them, and the roaring rivers have no outlet into the Kathmandu Valley. The Nepal Tourism Board, and practically everyone I speak to on the ground, is keen to highlight that the devastation is concentrated in a specific area, primarily the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and parts of Dhading district. The rest of Nepal, from popular trekking areas like Everest and Annapurna, and cities like Kathmandu and Pokhara, remains unaffected and open to visitors. Tourism is a major contributor to the country’s economy, and in 2025 Nepal welcomed 1.16 million visitors. Given the terrifying scenes witnessed on the news and social media, it’s natural that travelers with bookings to Nepal may be concerned about whether they should still come or not. But the message from the Nepal Tourist Board is unequivocal: Nepal is not closed. The country is open and eager to welcome visitors. On September 1, Khadak Raj Paudel, Nepal’s Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, made a heartfelt plea on Instagram for travelers to continue visiting and to stand with the country. “Our airports are still operating, our mountains, trails and trekking routes are still open to you. The hotels are welcoming you with open arms,” he said. “Travelling to Nepal at this time is not just a holiday. It’s a support.” It’s a sentiment echoed by Shrestha Einhaus. His hotels have seen a flurry of cancellations. “Tourism is one of the main economic drivers for Nepal, and is something that breathes life into the country,” he tells me. “That’s why it’s important to share where it’s safe to go, and where it’s not safe to go. The majority of the country is safe.” The best way to support Nepal right now is not to cancel your trip, and to plan your next visit, he says. Namgyal Sherpa, CEO of Sherpa Hospitality, a company operating mountain lodges and trekking expeditions in Everest, Annapurna, Mustang, Chitwan, and Lumbini, is also keen to reassure travelers that there is no need to cancel their trips if they are not going to directly affected areas. “We understand that people may feel overwhelmed by the amount of information and images circulating on social media, but it’s important to remember that these reports do not represent conditions across the entire country,” he says. “Our advice is not to cancel your travel plans, but to review your itinerary carefully and stay informed about local conditions.” Those with imminent travel should refer to the latest information from the Nepal Tourism Board, and coordinate with their on-the-ground hotels and organizers. A number of local and international aid organizations, including the Nepal Red Cross, World Central Kitchen, and Médecins Sans Frontières, are providing urgent relief and recovery operations. Locally, donations are being coordinated by the Government of Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, operating a “one-door” approach to ensure aid is distributed in an equal and organized manner, and to enable long-term restoration, resettlement, and rebuilding of communities, as well as immediate disaster relief. But in addition to making monetary donations, the message on the ground to those overseas who want to support Nepal in its time of crisis is clear. By visiting Nepal now and traveling in safe areas, you will be supporting the communities, workers, businesses, and families whose livelihoods depend on tourism. “Every person who comes to Nepal is making a contribution and having an impact on the broader community and those who rely on tourism for their income,” says Einhaus. Sherpa agrees. “Responsible tourism can be a powerful part of the recovery, and can provide important support to local communities and the tourism industry at a time when they need it most,” he says. “Nepal has always been a country of resilience, generosity, and community. We believe that with the support of people at home and around the world, the affected communities will recover, rebuild, and emerge stronger.”

item.title: Planning a Fall Foliage Trip? Book These Amtrak Routes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.17
A fall foliage train ride is the quintessential autumn getaway. US rail routes glide through some of the nation’s best scenery, including dense forests, glittering lakeshores, and rippling foothills. Even better: unlike a road trip through these colorful landscapes, a rail journey allows travelers to be completely absorbed in the bright red, orange, and yellow hues flicking past the windows. Amtrak trains stop in foliage-rich destinations across the US and Canada. And while the journey itself is certainly a highlight of the trip, travelers will also find seasonal attractions upon arrival at many of the routes’ stops, like apple picking, hikes through vibrant woodlands, and cozy stays at historical inns. Consider this your guide to booking a fall foliage train ride, from the best time to book for peak colors to the top Amtrak trains for reveling in all autumn has to offer. Simply buy your ticket, sit back, and enjoy Mother Nature’s awe-inspiring spectacle. This story has been updated with new information since its original publish date. What is the best time to plan a fall foliage train trip? Don’t forget that when planning a fall foliage trip, timing is key. You’ll want to visit your destination of choice when the changing leaves are decked out in their peak colors. There are several reliable online tools for predicting when the leaves will be the most vibrant. If you’re not sure where you want to visit, start with the Smoky Mountains fall foliage map, which shows predictions for the progression of the entire country’s leaves based on date. Another good choice is the Farmer’s Almanac, which lists the dates each state is predicted to reach peak foliage. Once you have your dates squared, these are the best Amtrak routes and destinations for an unforgettable fall foliage trip. Vermont Train line: Vermonter On its way from Washington DC to St. Albans, Vermont, Amtrak’s Vermonter train ambles through lush northeastern forests and charming small towns. (The entire 13-hour journey crosses nine states, from the Mid-Atlantic to New England.) Once in Vermont, you’ll have your pick of picturesque villages with plenty of fiery trees to view. The train's first stop in Vermont is a solid choice for a fall weekend getaway: the historic town of Battleboro. This pretty hamlet sits right on the Connecticut river in the foothills of the Green Mountains, so expect undulating blankets of colorful foliage in every direction. The train station is right in town, so most activities and amenities are accessible by foot. Stop by a local café or browse the shops lining Main Street. Rent a kayak from one of the local outfitters and gaze over the water toward hills filled with vibrant leaves. Or, head to nearby Fort Dummer State Park (about a 45-minute walk along South Main Street) for easy hiking trails and lookout points over crimson-tinged maple, oak, and birch trees. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Michigan Train line: Pere Marquette Amtrak’s Michigan Services are a series of rail lines running all throughout the Wolverine State. For an autumn sojourn, plan to hop aboard the Pere Marquette, a daily route that runs from Chicago to Grand Rapids. The train winds up Michigan’s west coast, offering brief but sweeping views of Lake Michigan and bisecting lush, Midwestern farmland dotted with trees resplendent in their autumn wardrobes. Once in Grand Rapids, the city’s 200+ local parks offer up-close views of nature’s shifting kaleidoscope. Among the highlights are Blanford Nature Center, which offers extensive walking trails through an old-growth forest of blazing red sugar maples. Don’t miss the Calvin Ecosystem Preserve and Native Gardens, with its network of scenic trails through more than 100 acres of forests and wetlands. The 1,500-acre Millennium Park is just five minutes from downtown Grand Rapids, yet is home to an 18-mile network of treelined trails that wind along lakes and rivers. After you’ve had your fill of forest-bathing, be sure to explore the local brewery scene for seasonal craft beers—after all, Grand Rapids is known as “Beer City, USA.” Fall-themed activities are available throughout the city as well. Don’t miss apple picking from century-old orchards at Robinette’s Apple Haus and Winery. Extend the historical charm to your accommodations with one of the area’s charming bed and breakfasts, like The Leonard at Logan House, which was built in 1914. Peak time for foliage: October 6 to 15 Wisconsin Train line: Empire Builder As Amtrak’s Empire Builder stretches from Chicago, across all of the Upper Midwest, and into Washington state, it offers plenty of foliage-centric destinations to choose from. Just under a four-hour ride from Chicago is a perfect locale for soaking in autumn’s glory: Wisconsin Dells. Head to Dells of the Wisconsin River State Natural Area for views of trees in their seasonal finery among numerous pines and set against Cambrian sandstone cliffs, canyons, and unique rock formations. Back in the center of town, a leisurely stroll along the scenic River Walk offers a chance to behold the bursts of color while weaving your way along the water. Unwind from all that hiking at one of the area’s local breweries. Then check into Sundara Inn & Spa, one of the first destination spas in the Midwest with treatments like Reiki and CBD massages. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October California Train line: California Zephyr Travelers looking for an extended fall train journey would do well to board Amtrak’s California Zephyr. The line stretches all the way from Chicago to Emeryville, California, in the Bay Area. But the scenery becomes especially dramatic once the train reaches Colorado and traverses the unique landscapes of the West. After passing through Denver, expect to ascend the Rockies, glide over Utah’s salt flats, past red rock canyons, and along the Sierra Nevadas. Hop off the train in Truckee, California, the gateway to the Lake Tahoe region, which transforms into a wonderland of colorful foliage come October. Here, visitors are treated to displays of yellows and reds as quaking aspens, willows, and cottonwoods morph into rich golds, ambers, and chartreuses, and oaks and dogwoods that add splashes of maroon and crimson, all contrasting with the mighty pines and deep blue lake. There’s no shortage of outdoor activities to soak in the autumnal atmosphere, either. Everything from mountain biking and kayaking, hiking and horseback riding will immerse travelers among the vivid trees. For a full outdoor experience, try camping at one of the numerous state-run sites along the lake’s perimeter, or opt for a bit of pampering at a resort and spa like the Hyatt Regency Lake Tahoe. Peak time for foliage: October 15 to 31 Maine Train line: Downeaster Amtrak’s Downeaster line weaves north from Boston through Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Maine, where it ends in the city of Brunswick. Expect smatterings of New England leaves to be on display throughout the journey. Hop off the train in Portland, about a two-hour ride from Boston. While there’s plenty to do in the city itself, we recommend taking a quick 15-minute ferry ride across Casco Bay to Peaks Island. The quaint island can be navigated by visitors without a car. Grab a bike or a golf cart at one of the rental shops in town or simply use your own two feet: the area is quite walkable. There’s one hotel on the island, The Inn on Peaks Island, and plenty of waterfront dining, making it a great choice for a quick overnight or weekend stay. Take a bike ride around the two-mile island loop to absorb the incredible views. The island has a mix of deciduous and evergreen trees, so you’ll get to see bursts of oranges and rubies as well as rich, dark greens, all set against a sparkling waterfront. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October Virginia Train line: Cardinal Whisking passengers through the Blue Ridge and Allegheny Mountains, the Amtrak Cardinal train offers a visual feast of fall colors. The U-shaped route curves down from New York City, swooping through 11 states and the District of Columbia before terminating in Chicago. Charlottesville, Virginia, is a stop along the way that’s perfectly situated for reveling in autumnal scenery. Seated smack dab in the middle of the Blue Ridge Mountains, the city is a fall wonderland come October. There are plenty of places in town to spot vibrant leaves, including the bosky campus of the University of Virginia and the historic Downtown Mall, which is pedestrian-only.
