But for the true leaf-peeping extravaganza, you’ll want to rent a car and head to Shenandoah National Park, about an hour’s drive away. Hike the easy 1.6-mile Stony Man loop to an awe-inspiring lookout point with a vista of the rolling hills of deciduous trees all around. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Montana Train line: Empire Builder Spanning eight states across the Northwestern US, the Empire Builder line operates from Chicago to Seattle and cuts through prime landscapes for foliage viewing. Leaf enthusiasts will want to hop off at Whitefish, Montana—a Rocky Mountain town that’s known for its access to Glacier National Park. Though the colors are spectacular, don’t expect to see rich reds or oranges. Here, it’s bright yellow tones that rule the day. Across the rolling hillsides and along the area’s scenic rivers, you’ll find brilliant honey-hued aspen trees and gold-tinged larches, a unique type of pine tree with needles that change from green to flaxen and fall away when the weather turns crisp. For the ultimate scenery, rent a car for a day and drive a quick 40-minute jaunt to Glacier National Park. There, you’ll see the resplendent larch trees framed by the park’s snow-capped peaks above and its sparkling lakes below. Drive the famous Going-to-the-Sun Road, which is less crowded in the fall months, to get a look at the most iconic views. Note that portions of the 50-mile road begin to close down in the third week of October, so be sure to check the official road status page for the latest information. Peak time for foliage: Mid-October Massachusetts Train line: Lake Shore Limited In the fall months, the Berkshires are a true leaf-peeping paradise. The rolling mountain landscape becomes an undulating patchwork quilt of searing scarlets, terracottas, vermillions, and more. Amtrak’s Lakeshore Limited route puts fall travelers right in the colorful action, with its stop in Pittsfield, Massachusetts. During the four-hour trip from Boston, the route passes through open countryside and picturesque towns until it enters Western Massachusetts after Springfield. Then, the train follows the Westfield river and trundles through dense forests bedecked in autumnal grandeur. Pittsfield station is located in the heart of the downtown district, so travelers can step off the platform and straight into charming shop-lined streets and walkable accommodations like the Hotel on North. Farther afield, there are cozy inns like The Old Inn on the Green in New Marlborough and 33 Main in nearby Lenox. Explore the region’s surrounding farms, like Bartlett’s Orchard for u-pick apples and extensive farmer’s markets at Berkshire Grown. For a deep-dive into the region’s vast foliage, try a longer hike along Yokun Ridge, which offers eight-miles of trails that connect Pittsfield and Lenox, with three lookout points over the tie-dyed treetops. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 21 Connecticut Train line: Northeast Regional One of Amtrak's most popular routes, the Northeast Regional train also doubles as a fall foliage express come October. Spanning from Virginia all the way to Boston, almost every stop is a chance to spot tie-dyed treetops. Hopping off in Connecticut—we recommend the charming town of Mystic— is a great bet to experience the wondrous effects of Mother Nature’s paint brush. Located right in Mystic is the Denison Pequotsepos Nature Center, which offers numerous hiking trails winding through forests of stately oaks, red maples, and American beech trees aflame with color. Heading a bit farther north (40 minutes by car) to the Pachaug State Forest will afford even more chances to soak in a bevy of autumnal hues. On its many miles of trails, you’ll meander through a cathedral of trees in metamorphosis. For a truly awe-inspiring view over the treetops, hike to the Mount Misery Overlook. Contrary to its name, this vista is sure to delight the foliage-minded among us. At 441 feet high, the lookout is the highest point of elevation in the area, meaning a bird’s eye view of the forest’s colorful canopy. At the end of the day, treat yourself to a seaside tipple at Mystic’s waterfront bar Red 36 or dinner at The Shipwright’s Daughter, which offers seasonal fare from local purveyors. Peak time for foliage: Mid- to late October Minnesota Train line: Borealis One of Amtrak’s newest lines is also among its best fall journeys. Launched in 2024, the Borealis train runs between Chicago and St. Paul-Minneapolis through historic small towns, Mississippi River bluff landscapes, and verdant farmlands of the Upper Midwest. Trees are plentiful along the route, with oaks, maples, birches, and more awash in a palette of oranges, yellows, and reds. Foliage-seekers can alight in the town of Winona, Minnesota, located on an island in the Mississippi—where visitors hike, kayak, or fish amid craggy river bluffs carpeted with ever-changing treetops. Key sites include the 3,000-acre Great River Bluffs State Park, whose hiking trails offer broad vistas over the colorful canopies and across the Mississippi and Black rivers; Sugar Loaf Bluff, a distinctive rock formation with hikes and advanced rock climbing; and Lake Park, with easy, paved trails encircling Lake Winona. Enjoy the foliage from the serenity of the river with a guided boat tour. Be sure to stay at a hotel with scenic views, too, like the boutique Hotel 44 Degrees North, located in the heart of downtown with rooms that overlook the river bluffs and forests. Peak time for foliage: October 5 to 20 Montreal Train line: Adirondack Restarting operations just in time for fall trips across the Canadian border is Amtrak’s full Adirondack line, which stretches from New York City to Montreal. The route was shuttered for six weeks over the summer in order to complete track modifications. It reopened to the public in early September. That’s good news for autumnal fanatics, as this foliage-rich route—lined with maples, oaks, birches, and more—becomes postcard-perfect each October. Expect multicolored arboreal panoramas to fill the giant picture windows as you weave through the Hudson River Valley, past Lake Champlain, and along the hills of the Adirondacks. Notable stops along the way include Hudson and Saratoga Springs in New York, but we recommend riding the entire 10-hour route to Montreal to absorb the full force of the fall ambience. Once in Montreal, there are plenty of options to continue the leaf-appreciation tour. Mount Royal, the famous mountain peak overlooking the city, will be a riot of color. Less than an hour outside the metro area are dazzling nature reserves chock full of morphing trees, like the Morgan Arboretum and Parc-Nature du Cap-Saint-Jacques. Peak time for foliage: Early to mid-October

item.title: Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The sophomore season expands beyond English country piles to Mafia-held Italian palazzos
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.12
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions were something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveller, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’s filming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: What does the EU's new hand luggage rule mean for travellers? Here’s everything you need to know about the updated air passenger rights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.11
On Tuesday 1 September, Members of the European Parliament confirmed changes to air passenger rights that were first reported earlier in 2026. These rules have been in place for more than 20 years, since 2004, and aim to protect passengers against disruption to their travels. While many of our rights, such as compensation if flights are delayed by a certain number of hours, will simply be upheld by the latest vote, there are some changes due to come into effect, too. Extra costs for hand luggage have been something that’s plagued travellers for decades, but new regulations are set to change that. After more than a decade of negotiations between the Council of the EU and the European Parliament, a landmark agreement has been reached. What is the new rule for hand luggage? New rules will include the right for passengers to carry one personal item such as a small bag or backpack with them onboard without incurring an extra cost. Airlines will also be required by law to display air fares that include carry-on luggage while booking to improve transparency and comparability between airlines and tickets. Airlines may still offer cheaper tickets who travel without hand luggage, MEPs say. A small catch to be aware of, however, is that this regulation applies to EU airlines only. This means that on non-EU airlines, like easyJet and Jet2, passengers may still be bound to the old regulations – except on flights returning to the UK from an EU country. Which other rights have been introduced? Several new rights are set to improve passenger safety and protection. These include rules to make it easier for passengers to claim compensation and access assistance in case of delay or cancellation, as well as new regulations reinforcing rights for persons with specific needs, such as persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and pregnant passengers. Air passenger rights changes to know - The right to carry on board, without extra cost, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack - Passengers will no longer be charged for correcting spelling errors or for a printed version of a boarding pass if they have already checked in - Passengers will be able to take the return flight of a two-way ticket even if they did not use the first flight - Clearer and quicker reimbursement for flight disruption and travel delays - Passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility will have the right to compensation, rerouting and assistance if they miss a flight due to the airport’s failure to help them reach the gate on time - Any person accompanying a child below the age of 14 will be entitled to an adjacent seat without paying extra. The same right will apply to passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility, and to pregnant women. “I’m proud that, after 13 years of negotiations, we reached a landmark agreement to strengthen EU air passenger rights,” announced Alexis Vafeades, minister of transport, communications and works of the Republic of Cyprus. “This modernised framework will deliver certainty, fairness and stronger protection for millions of European air passengers. The agreement strikes a fair balance for our airlines, helping preserve connectivity that is vital to the EU’s internal market and its citizens.”

item.title: Flying with children is about to get cheaper and easier thanks to new EU rules – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.89
Ever found yourself fuming that in order to ensure you get a seat next to your child on the way to your family holiday, you have to pay extra for a seat for each of you – on top of what's probably an already hefty ticket price? You're not alone. But changes to EU air passenger rights will make this annoyance a thing of the past, as the right for children under the age of 14 to sit next to an accompanying adult free of charge will be protected. In September 2026, Members of the European Parliament approved changes to rules on air passenger rights that have been protected since 2004. There's a slate of changes due to come into force, but the parents among the Condé Nast Traveller team were particularly intrigued by the promise that a free adjacent seat will be guaranteed for a child under the age of 14 and the adult accompanying them. That means airlines cannot split up families at seat allocation, and cannot charge you extra to sit together. Why under the age of 14? For most airlines, children under 14 cannot travel without an accompanying adult on the same flight. The change means that adding extra fees to allow parents and children to sit together – which can quickly add up as they're charged per person – will be a thing of the past. The rules come into effect 12 months and 20 days after their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union – around August 2027, just in time for any end-of-summer holidays. Other rights that will come into practice next August thanks to these include: - Making it easier to claim compensation if your flight is delayed or cancelled - Transparent pricing that displays ticket prices including cabin baggage by default - Personal items stored under the seat should be free of charge

item.title: Volcano eruption in Indonesia: the latest updates, government guidelines and travel advice
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.08
Late on Friday 4 September, Mount Anak Krakatau, located 150km from Jakarta, erupted continuously for 25 hours, producing fountains of lava and a booming sound that could be heard hundreds of kilometres away from the epicentre. According to Indonesia’s Geological Agency, the continuous eruption began at 11.07pm local time on Friday and ended 25 hours later, at 12.04am on Sunday 6 September. The volcano remains active today, with lighter, intermittent eruptions, prompting school closures and maintaining its Level III alert status. The Geological Agency confirmed that “the probability of additional eruptions in the coming days remains high”. “We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” said Lana Saria, head of the Geological Agency. Mount Anak Krakatau, which means "Child of Krakatoa", is located in the Sunda Strait, separating the islands of Java and Sumatra. Since it emerged from the sea about a century ago in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa, it has been sporadically active. In 2018, the collapse of Anak Krakatau triggered a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java, but, according to Saria, the most recent series of eruptions does not have the potential to trigger a tsunami. The main hazards for visitors and locals are volcanic ash, high gas concentrations, and the ejection of hot rocks, lava, and other material around the crater area. Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and sits in a seismic area prone to earthquakes and tsunamis. Indonesia lies along the Pacific ‘Ring of Fire’, a belt of seismic activity around the Pacific Ocean that contains around 75 per cent of the world’s active volcanoes. Travel disruption in Indonesia Volcanic ash is present in the airspace around Jakarta and several other cities, which prompted Indonesian authorities to close eight airports until 6pm Monday (local time), including Jakarta's international airports of Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma, Radin Inten in Lampung on Sumatra, and Husein Sastranegara in West Java. The situation is developing, so airport closures could therefore be extended further, depending on volcanic activity, as confirmed by transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi: “We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather.” So far, the natural disaster has disrupted around 2,300 flights and affected 270,000 passengers, who are now stranded in the country. Which airports are currently closed? - Halim Perdanakusuma Airport (HLP), Jakarta - Soekarno Hatta International Airport (CGK), Tangerang, serving Jakarta - Radin Inten II Airport (TKG), Lampung - Husein Sastranegara Airport (BDO), Bandung - Budiarto Airport (RTO), Curug, Tangerang - Pondok Cabe Airport (PCB), South Tangerang - Muhammad Taufiq Kiemas Airport, Pesisir Barat, Lampung - Atung Bungsu, South Sumatra Is it safe to travel to Indonesia? Air travel has been significantly disrupted in Jakarta and other affected parts of Java and Sumatra, with flights cancelled, delayed or diverted. Travellers should check the latest status of their flight directly with their airline or travel provider before travelling. The FCDO advises against all travel to certain areas but not the country as a whole; you can find the full list on the government website. If you decide to travel to Indonesia during this time, remember to check with your travel insurer to make sure your plan is still valid considering the circumstances.

item.title: Best eSIMs for travellers 2026: How to beat airport Wi-Fi and extortionate roaming fees for good, tried-and-tested by our editors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.90
On the list of additional costs that can trip up travellers, the dreaded roaming data charge is one of the most irritating. While there are usually phone plan kiosks or the odd SIM card vending machine at the airport, by the point you’ve reached the arrivals lounge, you’re a captive audience and beholden to whatever rate is offered. You also might need data before leaving the airport: I’m still scarred by the charge I incurred in the connecting terminal in Singapore when the WiFi wasn’t working and I needed to let my partner know I’d arrived. But there is a way to beat the charges before you’ve even left the country – and that’s by using an eSIM. Often, purchasing a dedicated travel SIM works out cheaper than buying the additional data bundles offered by your UK phone network, especially for frequent fliers and those headed further than Europe. Plus, by using a digital SIM rather than a physical one, there’s no need to wait for it to arrive or worry about losing your regular SIM card while it’s not in use. Below, we’ve outlined the best eSIM services to know in time for your next trip, along with the price for a week’s worth of data for a long-haul flight to Indonesia as a price comparison guide. The best eSims for travellers at a glance: - Best overall: Ubigi - Best for digital nomads: Saily - Best for customisable data top-ups: aloSIM - Best for heavy data users and longer stays: Holafly - Best pay-as-you-go eSIM: Roamless - Best value eSIM: Airhub - Best for app-free setup: easySim - Best for short trips: GoMo World - Best for security and extra perks: Yesim - Best for essential app-only coverage: Honest Mobile - Best for rewards and younger travellers: Global YO - Best for business travel: Maya Mobile Ubigi Best eSIM overall - Pros: Top-up possible without WiFi or data remaining, worldwide data plans, 5G available - Cons: Little pricier than some of the other services on our list for some countries - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6 Ubigi is a comprehensive data service for over 200 countries, with data plans from 500mb to unlimited. There are one-off, monthly and annual services, so digital nomads, business travellers and holidaymakers alike will all be covered. If you run out of data, you can top up without being connected to WiFi even without any remaining data, which is an additional safety boon that other services on this list can't always match. 5G connectivity is also available at no extra cost where possible. You can also save 10 per cent on prices on your first order with the code CNTRAVELLER. Editor review: I used a Ubigi eSim when I travelled to Yellowstone from London recently. I think the tell that a service like this is working well is to realise you don’t think about it at all. My internet in the States was just as speedy as when I’m in the UK, and worked as soon as I landed at Denver airport to await my transfer. I appreciate this as a lot of airports charge for WiFi or make you hunt down one of those tedious booths for a code before you’re granted the privilege to log on – if you can’t find one or it’s out of order, as happened to me in Hong Kong one time, then you’re either stuck internetless or have to suck it up and pay your network’s extortionate roaming fee. By activating my eSim immediately upon landing, I didn’t have to worry about connecting to the airport WiFi at all. But the main boon was being able to top up via the app even without being connected to WiFi. Wyoming is very large, very empty, and free fast WiFi was often in short supply. I was grateful to be able to top up without WiFi on one day trip – I didn’t realise I was running low on data before leaving and would have had a whole day without connectivity otherwise. This would have been anxiety-producing as a solo traveller very far from home! Charley Ward Saily Best eSIM for digital nomads - Pros: Good variety of plans, regional and global plans available - Cons: A little more expensive than some of the others listed - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.89 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.89 If you’re looking for data abroad, you’re sorted with Saily, whether you’re going on a quick three-day hop to longer three-month treks. You can buy per country or per region – handy if you’re island hopping across Asia, for example – and there are even worldwide plans for the most intrepid travellers. We like how seamless this service is, especially. You can purchase the data in the UK and when you arrive at your destination, it’ll switch on automatically, so you’re never without data and prevents being hit by accidental roaming charges in the airport. Saily has unlimited data plans in 37 destinations including the US, Japan, France, Spain, Italy and Thailand, plus an unlimited European data plan that works in 36 European countries. The app also has various tours and experiences bookable within the Saily app dependent on where you're headed. New users can use code CNT10 for 10 per cent off all mobile data plans worldwide. aloSIM Best for customisable data top-ups - Pros: Easy-to-use app, transparent pricing, flexible data top-ups without hidden fees - Cons: Data-only plans (no traditional phone calls or SMS) - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: Approx. £8.20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: Approx. £6.70 If you prefer straightforward, data-only coverage without signing up for unnecessary bells and whistles, aloSIM is a reliable contender. It operates across more than 170 countries, is easy to set up via the minimal mobile app – which allows you to calculate and purchase the exact amount of data you’ll need before stepping onto the plane; not something that can be said of all of the brands featured here. Installation is instant via a quick QR code scan and topping up takes mere seconds in the app should you run out of data or your trip is extended. One note: this brand’s eSims don’t support traditional voice minutes or SMS. However, for seamless 4G/5G connectivity for internet-based messaging apps, navigation, and streaming, it’s a worthy choice. Holafly Best for heavy data users and longer stays - Pros: Unlimited data packages in most destinations, 24/7 customer support, customisable plan durations - Cons: Considerably higher price point if you’re taking short trips, limited hotspot capabilities on some plans - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for Indonesia: Approx. £20.40 - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for USA: Approx. £20.40 For travellers who refuse to count megabytes or hunt down hotel WiFi, Holafly is the go-to provider. Rather than capped data tiers, Holafly built its reputation on offering unlimited data plans across 180+ destinations – essentially, wherever you are in the world, this is the eSim for you. You can tailor your package to the exact length of your trip – whether that’s three days or a full month – ensuring you never pay for extra days you don’t need. It is undeniably pricier upfront than fixed-data alternatives, but for remote workers, heavy video streamers, or anyone who relies heavily on maps and ride-hailing apps on the move, should find the peace of mind worth the investment. Roamless Best pay-as-you-go eSim - Pros: Pay-as-you-go data options ensures no wasted data, voice calls available, well priced - Cons: Although potentially more convenient, pay-as-you-go plans can work out more expensive than fixed plans - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.70 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.70 It’s a problem I’ve had when travelling a couple of times: you have to top up your eSim a day or so before the end of your trip, but then leave the country without using all the new data, thus wasting it (and, therefore, the money you paid for it). Not so with Roamless, which has pay-as-you-go options that won’t expire after 30 days. That means if you don’t burn through all your data on your trip, you can use it on your next getaway, even if you’re not returning to the same destination. The brand also has regular data packages for over 200 countries worldwide from free 500MB packs up to to 20GB, as well as packages including call-time, all for a very reasonable price point that’s lower than some of our other favourites on this list. You can save 20 per cent on your first purchase with the code CNT20. Airalo - Pros: 200+ destinations, regional and global deals, great connection - Cons: highest prices on our list, most packs are data-only - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Habits are hard to break, and I must admit I was sceptical about using my first eSIM. But after one-too-many surprise phone bills, I finally decided to take the leap during a sunny Croatia break, and where better to start than the world’s first and largest eSIM provider: Airalo. Steady Wi-Fi for around twenty minutes is necessary for installing the eSIM, so I’d recommend doing so before you travel, but you can activate the actual data plan within minutes once you land. Airalo’s easy-to-follow setup guide clearly directed me through the process, and I quickly found myself connected to my new data plan – with noticeably improved connection. I was staying in an off-grid beach village near Dubrovnik, and while my travel buddy struggled for internet access in our hotel room, my connection was fast and reliable at all times. Editor review: The sim is all based around Airalo’s no-frills mobile app, where you can flick through the loaded catalogue of national, regional, and global packs. My 3GB package (priced at £7.50) turned out to be plenty for a five-day trip, but the app also provides instant data top-ups in case you run out. It’s worth noting that almost all Airalo packages are data-only, so text and calls have to be supplied through your original provider, but for me, this feature was ideal. With the eSIM neatly slotting alongside my physical sim, there was no need for the confusing chore of switching phone numbers, and so this eSIM lived up to the hassle-free hype in all areas. Layla Quaedvlieg. Airhub Best value eSIM - Pros: Yearly and monthly subscriptions, unlimited data and voice options available - Cons: None that we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £4.75 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £2.37 This is our best value eSIM option – Airhub is a great service for frequent travellers and digital nomads especially. The app is intuitive and easy to use, and there are plenty of different plans available for trips of all lengths. One perk this service offers over the others we like is the yearly and monthly subscriptions, which make financially savvy options for those on longer trips – for example if you’re stationed somewhere for work or taking advantage of that post-Covid ‘work from anywhere’ lifestyle. There are also plans that include voice minutes and SMS services, which is an additional boast that the other services here can’t match. Editor review: On a recent work trip, I realised how useful the combined voice and data plans can be when travelling. In the UK I rarely make traditional voice calls, but on this particular trip I needed to connect with a contact that didn’t use WhatsApp, so I couldn’t make a call over the internet. I’ve a spend cap on my regular sim which, as I learned, prevented me from making calls abroad. I was left in a frustrating situation where I wasn’t quite sure how to get hold of the guy. The problem was resolved by downloading this eSim, and also meant I didn’t have to spend time removing and then re-adding the spend cap on my regular plan when I got home. If you travel a business and make a lot of calls, I’d recommend this eSim. Charley Ward EasySim - Pros: Diverse range of data plans, many plans work across multiple countries, no need for an app - Cons: No family feature for managing multiple eSIMS per account - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £8.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Editor review: EasySim is part of the EasyJet family of brands, so they know a thing or two about roaming. True to form, it’s one of the most comprehensive services on offer, with a good range of plans at some of the best prices we’ve seen. Some may not like the lack of an app, but the website is easy to use and does the job perfectly well. As a bonus, this service covers a wide range of phones. Not all the options on this list are compatible with my Motorola – an admittedly niche handset – so the compatibility here adds an additional sweetener to this service for me. GoMo World Best eSIM for short trips - Pros: Low starting prices - Cons: Fewer cross-country compatible plans than EasySim, calls, SMS and MMS services aren’t currently provided - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: No 3GB plan available; 1.5GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: No 3GB plan available; 1GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 As someone who travels regularly for work, and often only for a few days at a time, I’ve sometimes found myself paying over the odds for week-long data plans when I’m only away a few days. Case in point on a recent trip to the Maldives, where I was beholden to the airport’s singular 10gb data SIM offering despite only being in the country for three days. So, if you’re one for regular short hops, GoMo World’s smaller plans are ones to consider for maximum cost-saving benefits. Yesim - Pros: Coverage in 200+ destinations worldwide and a ‘refer a friend’ rewards system to save money on data plans. - Cons: Connection speeds limited to local carrier availability - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: 3GB £9 for 30 days, 5GB £11.70 for 15 days, 10GB £19.80 for 30 days - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: 3GB not available, 500MB for 0.45p for 3 days, 10GB £14.40 for 30 days, 15GB £16.20 for 30 days This Swiss-based eSIM provider boasts excellent reviews on Trustpilot and with good reason. The broad, global coverage offers fast, consistent internet activity in over 200 countries, is easy to use and set up, and is reasonably priced with no hidden extras. The built-in VPN technology offers enhanced security and reassurance when travelling, while the fast customer support service is there ready to answer any questions or fix problems, should they arise, with ease. We’re impressed by the virtual phone number rental capability, too – a rare addition among eSIM providers. Honest Mobile - Pros: Perfect if you’re only planning on using apps rather than making calls. - Cons: Doesn’t support internet calling or streaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming This smart SIM automatically switches to EE, O2, or Three when your main SIM loses signal and provides free, unlimited global roaming for over 200 essential apps, including Google Maps, Skyscanner, and Uber, across 180+ countries. This eliminates the stress of data caps and roaming charges while on your travels. It’s a great idea for keeping costs low, just be careful to stick within the limits of what this eSIM can offer. Maya The best eSIM for business travel - Pros: Money-back guarantee for 180 days, high-speed internet connection, global packages - Cons: None as far as we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: From £5.39 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: From £7.19 For a solid choice with no hidden fees, Maya is a good option. No contracts, 24/7 customer service, and a money back guarantee for up to 180 days. This means that if disaster strikes and your trip is cancelled, you can request an immediate refund with no extra charges. The SIMs are compatible with IOS and Android devices, and with at least two (if not more) networks available in each destination, the 4G/5G internet truly is high-speed. We love their new global eSIM package too, which includes across 119 destinations and starts from as low as £4.79, as well as the special business options, revolutionising the company work trip with shared data pooling. FAQs How we tested the best eSims To find the best travel eSIMs, our editors tested a variety of eSims across a range of long-haul and short-haul trips – from quick European city breaks to multi-stop journeys through Asia and North America. We evaluated how straightforward the provider’s app and setup process was, measuring how quickly we could download, install, and activate data profiles before departure. Once on the ground, we put network reliability, download speeds, and signal strength to the test in a variety of locations, including busy airport arrival lounges, remote countryside, and dense city centres. Finally, we compared overall value for money, flexibility, data-top-up ease, and customer support responsiveness. What is an eSIM? In plain English, it’s a virtual sim card that you install via an app rather than by inserting a physical card into your phone. They are activated remotely, so there’s no need to visit your local phone shop or wait for it to arrive. In your phone’s settings, you’ll be able to toggle between your existing physical sim card and the eSim, even being able to use both simultaneously, such as using one for mobile data and the other for calls and texts. This is handy if your eSim plan is data only but you’d still like the phone and SMS capability while away. It means that, if you download and install the eSim before you head off, you can activate it in the airport when you land and beat pricey roaming charges forevermore. The setup is simple. After registering online, all it takes is a quick scan of a QR code and you’re good to go. If you run out of data, you don’t need to download a new one – just top up your existing plan. Each eSIM has its own inclusions, from calls, texts, and internet streaming, to exclusive access to essential apps like Google Maps, so make sure to check in advance which plan best suits your needs. If that’s not enough to convince you, the entirely virtual setup means that they are also kinder to the planet than the plastic chips of traditional SIMs. Is my phone eSim compatible? Most Apple iPhone, Google Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy models released in the UK since 2018 are eSIM compatible. For other smartphones, the quickest way to check eSIM compatibility is by dialing *#06# on your phone's keypad – a screen pop-up including an EID number indicates your device is eSIM-friendly. You will also need to make sure that your device is not locked to a single network. If this is the case, provided you’ve reached the end of your original contract, you can ask your provider to unlock it for free by requesting a Network Unlock Code (NUC). Do I need a different eSIM for each country I visit? No. All eSIMs are suitable for use worldwide, so you’ll only need to install one eSIM. Do check, however, that the eSim provider you select has data plans available for the country you want to visit – all of the brands below have hundreds of countries available, so this shouldn’t be a problem in the vast majority of instances. Some plans are suitable for use in multiple countries, too, which is good if you’re taking a longer trip hopping from place to place – like if taking a cruise, for example. Airalo, for instance, has packages valid for use in up to 137 countries, from Jamaica to Japan.

item.title: 11 most beautiful autumn train journeys in Europe that encourage slow travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.61
Summer is a gorgeous time to enjoy train-hopping on France’s Mediterranean coast (the Train de la Côte Bleue is a journey you must add to your summer 2027 bucket list) or southern Italy on a regional train from Naples to Reggio Calabria – but autumn is arguably the best time to visit Europe by train. While summer sees hordes of tourists travelling from around the world, putting pressure on rail networks and often making a train trip feel like a sauna, autumn – as well as spring – allows you to visit even some of the continent’s most popular destinations with a little more ease and comfort. While Switzerland and Italy may be the ultimate destinations for scenic train travel, there are routes across Europe that combine fabulous scenery with interesting sights and activities at both ends of the journey. We have gathered some of the best train rides across Europe to give you some ideas for your next train adventure. Italy Train line: Vigezzina Centovalli Railway Italians love to complain about their railway system, but the truth is Italy has one of the best – if not the best – train travel offerings in Europe. Simple regional trains often offer fabulous views over the Italian countryside and coastlines – my yearly train from Naples to Paola is one of my favourite summer activities – but there are some specific routes that deserve the detour. The Vigezzina-Centovalli Railway connects Domodossola in Italy to Locarno in Switzerland in around two hours, passing through the striking Vigezzo Valley and the Centovalli (Hundred Valleys) and allows travellers to stop and visit charming villages such as Santa Maria Maggiore or impressive sites like the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Sangue in Re. In autumn, the service becomes known as the ‘Foliage Train’. Just note that the special foliage ticket allows one intermediate stop on either the outward or return journey, rather than unlimited hopping on and off, so choose wisely. Switzerland Train line: GoldenPass Belle Époque (from Montreux to Zweisimmen) When it comes to scenic train routes, Switzerland always makes it to the top of the list. Out of the many famous routes, the Bernina Express is probably the most popular, but I think that is a route that can wait for winter. Instead, autumn is the perfect time of year to book a GoldenPass Belle Époque train and admire some truly stunning Swiss foliage while sitting in vintage 1930s-style carriages. This route takes travellers from Montreux to Zweisimmen in around two hours through the Gruyère district and the Pays-d’Enhaut. The carriages have panoramic windows, offering uninterrupted views of lakes, mountain peaks and forests along the way.T Greece Train line: Odontotos Rack Railway (Diakopto to Kalavryta) Greece is more popular for boat-powered island hopping than for train travel, but the country has a few gorgeous routes up its sleeve. If finding an unspoiled Greek island is becoming more and more difficult, the Peloponnese region is still fairly under the radar and has a lot to offer year-round. The Odontotos Rack Railway from Diakopto to Kalavryta takes around one hour and shows you a different side of Greece, following the Vouraikos River through its dramatic gorge. Take this opportunity to enjoy a few days in Diakopto, a lovely seaside town usually still sunny and warm in autumn, before getting a complete change of scenery when arriving in the mountain town of Kalavryta. France Train line: Strasbourg to Sélestat via Molsheim, Obernai and Barr (following the Route des Vins d'Alsace) If there is one event that defines autumn in Europe, it is the wine harvest, and France has a fabulous train route to celebrate this time of year by rail. The Route des Vins d’Alsace winds through eastern France and offers a wonderful introduction to the Alsace wine region. There are a few itineraries that can be created following this route but, if it’s your first time in the region, starting from the beautiful city of Strasbourg seems like a good option. From there, take the Strasbourg-Sélestat line that runs through vineyards and allows you to stop in some charming towns such as Molsheim, Obernai and Barr. From early August to mid-October, wine villages across the region host a packed calendar of harvest festivals and events, so make sure you check the calendar and organise your visit to coincide with an event that catches your eye. Portugal Train line: Douro Valley Line (Linha do Douro) The Linha do Douro is a 160-kilometre historic line that connects the city of Porto to the village of Pocinho, running alongside the Douro River, and crossing 35 bridges along the way. The one-way trip is three hours and twenty minutes, but the full journey can still be tackled as a day trip, returning to Porto the same evening. If you don’t feel like committing to a seven-hour train journey in a day, you could stop in the charming town of Pinhão for a wine tasting at Quinta do Bomfim or Quinta das Carvalhas. It cuts one hour off the journey each way and you can still do it in one day if you take the morning train from Porto and make sure you are back in time to take the last train back to the city from Pinhão station. Serbia and Montenegro Train line: Belgrade to Bar If you thought that the Balkans didn’t have great train routes, the trip from Belgrade to Bar will change your mind. With its eleven hours and 476 kilometres, this is a very long train journey that takes travellers from the green hills of Serbia to the rugged mountains of Montenegro. The journey can be made on an overnight service year-round, while a daytime train operates seasonally. In 2026, it runs until 30 September, although it’s worth checking the operator’s website before travelling as timetables can change. Of course, the morning train is the one to take to be able to fully enjoy the views through the Dinaric Alps. The railway crosses 435 bridges – the most spectacular being the 498-metre-long Mala Rijeka Viaduct, which rises almost 200 metres above the valley floor. This is neither the quickest nor the most comfortable train ride you can take in Europe, but it’s definitely worth it if you are passionate about train travel. Norway Train line: Flåm Railway Not only is this one of the most beautiful train journeys in Europe year-round, but in good Norwegian fashion, the route is extremely well organised for tourists who want to enjoy everything that the area has to offer. You can simply book your train tickets and enjoy the ride, or choose a package that includes excursions and accommodation through Norway in a Nutshell. The train journey is twenty kilometres long and lasts around one hour one way, taking you through peaks, valleys, waterfalls and rivers. From cycling, hiking and swimming to ziplining, there is a lot to do along the way so you can spend one day or a full week exploring. Austria Train line: The Arlberg Railway This train route connects the Austrian cities of Innsbruck and Bludenz and is 136 kilometres long, with direct trains completing the journey in around one hour and 45 minutes. During this time, you will speed through charming Alpine villages, rivers and steep-sided valleys framed by mountain peaks. If you are travelling from Innsbruck, this is only one of the many stunning train routes you can take around Austria, to Switzerland or through South Tyrol all the way to Italy, but it’s an ideal option if you want maximum scenery without committing to a full day on the rails. Germany Train line: West Rhine Railway If you are looking for a train journey that will immerse you in nature but want a less obvious alternative to the Alpine railways of Switzerland and Italy, consider Germany’s West Rhine Railway. The route stretches for 185 km, starting from Cologne and arriving at Mainz via Bonn, Koblenz, and Bingen. Cologne makes an excellent starting point, with its Gothic cathedral and lively riverside neighbourhoods worth exploring before you board. The two-hour journey is stunning from beginning to end, but the highlight is the Rhine Gorge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site visible from the train. Bulgaria Train line: Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway This train from Septemvri to Dobrinishte runs four times a day year-round, takes about five hours for the one-way trip, and costs only a few euros. This route is the closest thing in the Balkans to an Alpine train ride, winding through the valleys and gorges of the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope mountains and stopping at Avramovo, the highest railway station in the Balkans. If you want to stop anywhere during your trip, make it the town of Velingrad, the country’s most popular thermal spa destination.

item.title: The 10 best things to do in London this weekend
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.39
When searching for the best things to do in London this weekend, it’s hard not to end up more confused and indecisive than when you started. While it’s never a bad idea to secure a booking at one of the best restaurants in the capital, spend an evening in one of the latest innovative bars on the scene or even explore an iconic London attraction, we’re always on the lookout for new, exciting pop-ups, openings and events. Each week, we get the inside track on exciting things to do in London for the upcoming weekend to help us discover a new area of the city or explore a new address in a neighbourhood we thought we’d already uncovered. Things to do in London this weekend (11 - 13 September) 1. Savour a Sunday feast with a difference Sundays from 6 September If things still feel a little too balmy for a Sunday roast, make your way to Manteca, where Chris Leach’s team are serving special spreads sure to banish the dreaded scaries. The new, regularly changing menus are inspired by the family feasts Chris devoured during his journeys through Rome and Naples, designed to be enjoyed by groups. Think starters such as olives stuffed with Italian sausage and seafood fritto miso, followed by a large centrepiece such as a hearty tray of lasagne or spaghetti and meatballs, to be passed around. It’s great news for oenophiles, too, as head of wine Emily Acha Derrington is uncorking different magnums each weekend and pouring glasses all afternoon long. Address: Manteca, 49-51 Curtain Road, London EC2A 3PT Website: mantecarestaurant.co.uk 2. Dine as DJs play in a superclub 9 - 10 September There is no shortage of supper clubs in the capital right now – but just the one set to take place within an iconic superclub this weekend. Last Orders is a one-of-a-kind dining experience set to transform the Ministry of Sound’s dancefloor into a dining destination in celebration of the club’s 35th anniversary. Michelin-starred chef Brad Carter and renowned DJ Ralph Lawson are guiding guests through three decades of house music via a curated five-course menu in the heart of the nightclub. Expect dishes such as Chicago-style pizza filled with braised squid and spicy nduja and a refined take on the Berlin lamb kebab, inspired by the city's after-hours food scene. Address: Ministry of Sound, 103 Gaunt Street, London SE1 6DP, United Kingdom Website: ministryofsound.com 3. Check out the city’s new adults’ playground Open now Looking for a buzzy new hangout in the city? Look no further than Roxy Ballroom Holborn, which, following its official opening, promises flowing cocktails with a side of competitive chaos. Crazy pool, high-tech darts, basketball hoops, ping pong tables and karaoke booths are just a few of the activities on offer across the 12,000 square foot site, while the bar serves an array of tangy concoctions and American-style bites. Address: Roxy Ballroom Holborn, 246 High Holborn, London WC1V 7BN Website: roxyleisure.co.uk 4. Discover the delights of Iceland 10 - 12 September If an adventure to the Land of Fire and Ice has ever appealed, the inaugural Taste of Iceland festival is one for you this weekend. Following successful runs in more than 20 different cities around the world, the three-day cultural spectacular celebrates all things Icelandic across food, wellness and entertainment pop-ups. Address: Various events, across London Website: inspiredbyiceland.com 5. Keep festival season going 12 September Despite all the talk of pumpkin-spiced lattes among autumn-lovers, festival season isn’t over just yet. Emerge East is the hottest ticket in town this week, as DJ AG headlines the free East London festival returning to Barking Riverside this Saturday. Having built a huge following through his viral livestreams and surprise appearances from the likes of Skepta, Central Cee and Jorja Smith, DJ AG is joined by a stellar line-up on stage. In addition to the music, there’s plenty to do throughout the day, including Katie Bracher’s Riverside Sauna, inviting festival-goers to enjoy global bathing rituals, heat, cold contrast and steam. Address: Barking Riverside Station, Barking IG11 0DS Website: eventbrite.co.uk 6. Celebrate Asian culture beside the Thames 11 - 13 September Battersea Power Station is the place to be for foodies as Celebrasia returns this weekend. London’s largest South East Asian festival sees more than 40 restaurants run by established names and rising stars line up along the riverside, including returning favourites such as Eat Lah and Old Chang Kee. In addition to the gourmet spreads, there are more cultural happenings than ever before, including a new-for-2026 Film Festival, live music, dance, national dress parades and expert panel talks. Address: Battersea Power Station Riverside Website: batterseapowerstation.co.uk 7. Get smokey at Borough Market 10 September Turn up the heat on Thursday as Borough Market goes after-hours. Flame and Smoke is the brand-new evening event celebrating the theatre and flavour of cooking over fire, uniting the iconic market’s expert traders, chefs and restaurants for an al fresco evening of flame-cooked dishes spanning global cuisines, with DJs soundtracking the proceedings. Address: Borough Market, SE1 1TL Website: boroughmarket.org.uk 8. Listen in at Kings Place 3 - 13 September The London Podcast Festival returns for its 11th edition this year, pulling audiences into Kings Place, the city’s home of live podcasting, as a jam-packed schedule spans almost two weeks. Opening weekend’s highlights include Thursday evening's The World’s Coolest Disabled, as journalist and broadcaster Jordan Jarrett-Bryan discusses disability through a fresh, funny and unfiltered lens, and Chart Music: The TOTP Podcast on Saturday. Address: Kings Place, 90 York Way, London N1 9AG Website: kingsplace.co.uk 9. Savour BBQ flavours at The Ned 4 September - 4 October Swanky London hotel The Ned welcomes two Michelin-starred barbecue chefs for a month of flame-kissed flavours from this Saturday. John Bates from InterStellar BBQ and Ali Clem from la Barbecue transform The Ned’s Electric Bar and Diner with Texan scents and flavours, serving a menu showcasing the craftsmanship, provenance and bold flavours that have made Austin one of the world's tastiest destinations. Think sharing trays uniting highlights from each restaurant’s menu, packed with treats such as peach tea-glazed pork belly, tender pulled lamb shoulder, chimichurri beef short rib and chopped cheese sausage. Address: Electric Bar & Diner, The Ned London, 27 Poultry, City of London Website: thened.com 10. Catch Fringe favourites in Soho 1 - 26 September There’s good news for anyone suffering from Edinburgh Fringe FOMO, as the return of Underbelly Soho’s Fridge Fix sees a handpicked selection of the festival’s most talked-about shows land in the capital this month. Trojan comedy Burning Down The Horse kicks things off on Tuesday evening following two sell-out Fringe runs, while Thursday’s Never Let Go: An Unauthorised Retelling of James Cameron’s Titanic is a queer spectacular that condenses the tragedy into a captivating hour. This weekend’s highlights include Penelope, which reimagines the tale of Odysseus’ wife as she speaks her truth, and Raves R Us, which follows Charlie and his friends as they transform an abandoned warehouse and the theatre into a ravers' paradise for the evening. Website: underbellyboulevard.com

item.title: 12 authors on the books that inspired them to travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.04
Reading a good book can be a way to unwind after a stressful week at work, a way to escape reality for a little while, and a way to learn more about the world around us. However, books can also serve as some indirect inspiration for travel too – especially when a writer has transported you to a particular place or environment. I had this very experience recently whilst reading Carley Fortune’s latest romance novel, Our Perfect Storm. She’s an author who uses location as a character in itself and writes about it so beautifully, and this book has made me want to visit Tofino in Canada. And I’m not the only one who has been inspired by reading to plan or visit a new destination. To aid with your holiday planning, we asked a group of authors to tell us about the books that inspired them to travel to somewhere new and why. Dalia Al-Dujaili recommends Little Women by Louisa May Alcott When I was in New York alone for the first time in 2023, I decided to spend a few days exploring Boston and New England. I had romanticised ideas of the East Coast from my American Literature degree – The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, Little Women, and the poetry of Robert Frost and Mary Oliver. So I boarded a 6am Greyhound to Boston – very main character! – with no money and barely anything to eat except nuts and American trail mix. Five hours later, I checked into a random hostel, completely unprepared but enjoying the spontaneity. The next day, I had planned to take a ferry to Provincetown, where Mary Oliver lived, but a storm cancelled the ferries. Instead, I took the train to Salem. It was late October, so the town was full of pumpkins and candlelit New England houses. I spent the next few days exploring forests, visiting Louisa May Alcott’s house, browsing vintage bookshops, and eating lobster rolls. It was one of the best trips I’ve ever taken alone! Dalia Al-Dujaili is the author of Babylon, Albion Julia Armfield recommends Solo Faces by James Salter Solo Faces is perhaps one of the most compelling novels I've ever read about the combined ugliness and beauty of climbing. His passages about the cruelty and yet astonishing grace to be found in the Alps are just incredible and made it more or less imperative for me to visit the Swiss Alps myself. Travelling entirely by train from London enables you to witness an outrageous cross-section of landscapes and really adds to the sense that you are growing incrementally further and further away from reality, the higher up you get. Julia Armfield is the author of Our Wives Under The Sea and Up To The Light Sian Meades-Williams recommends The Stone Boudoir by Teri Maggio I bought this book on a slight whim from a bookshop in Greenwich, where the author visited because her grandmother said there was ‘nothing there’, and I not only completely fell in love with Sicily but wanted to see it for myself. It was incredible; I’ve been back a few times since my first trip and my partner and I even got engaged in that tiny town with ‘nothing to see’. Sian Meades-Williams is the author of The Pyjama Myth Beth Ashley recommends Fault Lines by Emily Itami The writing is so beautiful in the way it describes the environment of Tokyo you honestly feel like you can see it. Itami is so descriptive and romantic in her prose, and having the main character have a job where she shows people around is such a brilliant narrative device, also showcasing Tokyo to the reader. And when I finally took a trip to Tokyo, I ended up re-reading Fault Lines. Beth Ashley is the author of Sluts Tahmina Begum recommends Without Reservations by Alice Steinbach Without Reservations is a memoir by a Pulitzer-winning journalist and single working mother. At the time of writing, Steinbach’s children had grown up, her nest empty and there is a level of contentment with her career, while a level of discontentment with her life. The date marked in the library stamp at the front says I took this out on 3 April 2018. I would have been 23. Although Steinbach was writing on the other side of life, I vividly remember the impact this book had on me. My own version of Eat, Pray, Love. In fact, my first solo trip to Malta came shortly after this. I may not have lived as long as Steinbach when reading Without Reservations, but I had at that point been interning and working a few writing jobs in newsrooms, all at the same time, for already five years by then. I was similarly becoming more content in my career decisions while feeling, as though I was not living enough. So I did what many South Asian Muslim women are not asked to do that Steinbach was also seeking: joyful memories that were just for herself. Tahmina Begum is the author of Womanhood Rioghnach Robinson recommends Outline by Rachel Cusk It's been five years since I visited Greece, and longer since I first read Rachel Cusk's Outline, so I can't remember whether the book's diamond-cut Mediterranean descriptions really did drive me to Athens. But I do remember landing in 115-degree heat as that summer's wildfires bore down on the city, and the tinkling music in the sprawling, deserted restaurants near the scorching beach, and a long, one-sided conversation with a stranger about the organisation of Greek transit. So: Rachel Cusk clearly made Athens feel like Outline to me, and now, when I reread, Outline feels like that summer's Athens. Rioghnach Robinson is the author of Bad Words Stephanie Wrobel recommends Misery by Stephen King Misery inspired me to write my own cat-and-mouse thriller set in the publishing industry, but instead of an author held captive by his number-one fan, Revenge Plot pits a literary agent against an unhinged aspiring writer. I knew I needed somewhere suitably remote to trap them together, which led me to an Airbnb treehouse in the Catskill Mountains in New York and eventually to spending a few nights there alone for research. The reality was more unsettling than I’d anticipated. The treehouse had no cell service, and its walls were made of glass. It was beautiful during the day; after dark, all I could think about was how easily someone could be standing among the trees, watching me. Needless to say, plenty of that unease found its way into the book. Stephanie Wrobel is the author of Revenge Plot Fiona Valpy recommends The Weight Of Water by Anita Shreve I love Anita Shreve’s books set along the New England coastline. The Weight of Water is a dual-timeline novel about a historical murder and a contemporary relationship in freefall on the mysterious Isles of Shoals in the Gulf of Maine. I’m planning a trip there next year to explore more of the coast, and to visit Celia Thaxter’s beautiful garden. She was a poet who made her summer home on one of the rocky and inhospitable islands, planting a garden that inspired some of the paintings by the American Impressionist painter Childe Hassam. Fiona Valpy is the author of Sisters of the Midnight Sun Meg Charlton recommends Weetzie Bat by Francesca Lia Block If I said I moved to Los Angeles because of Weetzie Bat, I would not be alone. This is, apparently, a common reaction to reading Francesca Lia Block’s psychedelically overstuffed ode to the city. Block's LA is a smoggy, fizzy heaven for freaks and rebels, the young and young at heart, anyone willing to see the beauty glinting out between the strip malls and dying palms. A YA novel that flutters into magical realism might feel a tad overheated for some adult readers. But then again, LA can feel like that itself: Too big, too much. Sprawling and tacky and totally, utterly sublime. Meg Charlton is the author of Voyagers Charles Cumming recommends the James Bond series by Ian Fleming In the 1980s, as a pupil at the sort of cloistered boarding school with which Ian Fleming would have been familiar, I read every James Bond book going. 007 travelled far and wide – to the Bahamas and Japan, to Paris and Berlin – but it was the Istanbul of From Russia With Love that I longed to visit. Years later, researching a spy novel of my own, I finally came face-to-face with the crumbling Ottoman buildings, subterranean passages and magnificent mosques so vividly depicted in Fleming’s classic. Istanbul was crowded and sensual, a hub of skulduggery and corruption, still the perfect setting for a story of espionage. Charles Cumming is the author of ICARUS 17 Anna Deacon recommends The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd I've always been inspired by great travel writing, and my bookshelves are full of dog-eared Lonely Planet books that have travelled with me in a backpack to many far-flung places, but one book I return to time and time again is The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd. Even though I've spent a great deal of my life in the Cairngorms in Scotland and know the area really well, this book offers a whole different view of this rugged, wild landscape. Nan's writing is so visceral and descriptive, and her adventures inspire the reader to explore, not only these wild places, but themselves too. I've taken this book on so many adventures and it never stops inspiring me to plunge in icy river pools, quietly observe nature, and walk until I find myself. Anna Deacon is the author of The Wild Fix Scotland C.J. Tudor recommends The Shining by Stephen King The Shining is one of my favourite books and I’ve always wanted to visit the creepy Overlook Hotel featured in the film. In 2023, I travelled to Alaska to research my novel, The Gathering, and booked an isolated lodge in the mountains: Talkeetna Lodge. Everything about it, from the snowy mountain views to the huge lounge with its high vaulted ceiling, reminded me of the Overlook. It had only just opened for the season, so it was almost deserted, adding to the eerie feel, although disappointingly, the bartender was not called Lloyd! C.J. Tudor is the author of Serenity Falls

item.title: New London restaurants to try in September 2026: our editors' honest opinions on the openings everyone's talking about
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.54
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in September 2026 Bar Blondie, Queen's Park Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Address: 19-21 Lonsdale Road, NW6 6RA Website: barblondie.co.uk Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Oudh 1772, Borough Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry. Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Website: oudh1722.com Kismet, Borough Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening.
