item.title: The 3 Exercises That Will Save Your Legs on the Descent
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.67
(Photo: Canva) Most hikers think that the ascent up a mountain is the hardest part. But it’s the descent that your legs will remember the next day, especially every time you step down stairs or sit in a chair. As you place your foot on the ground, your quads absorb the impact and act like brakes, slowing your body down. This braking causes the soreness you’ll feel days later. If your quads fatigue early, it causes further stress on the muscles, ligaments, and tendons, which can lead to injury. The remedy for pain-free descents? Don’t think about strengthening certain muscles. Instead, think about preparing your body for the three actions it needs to perform going downhill: absorbing impact, controlling each step, and controlling the foot. Training these qualities three times a week over six to eight weeks leading up to your next backpacking trip can help your descents feel smoother, more controlled, and leave your legs fresher for the miles ahead. This exercise elevates the heels by a couple of inches, allowing the quads to work through a longer range of motion. By taking four seconds to lower into the squat, you can create the time under tension needed for the trail. Descending a trail is really thousands of controlled single-leg stability landings. The terrain, your balance, braking ability, coordination, and confidence will all affect how safely you can navigate a descent. One of the best gym exercises that carries over to hiking is the lateral step-down, which trains balance, eccentric control, and coordination, and boosts knee stability. It’s also a go-to for reducing knee pain during downhill hiking. The tibialis anterior, or shin muscle, works in a couple of ways during each step. One job is to lift the toes to clear obstacles such as rocks or roots. Its other role is to slow your foot down after your heel touches the ground; it’s basically a brake that keeps your foot from slapping the ground with each step. Long descents can leave this muscle sore because the toes land below the heel with each step, increasing the range of motion. This exercise helps strengthen and stabilize the muscles around the foot and ankle so you can descend pain-free. To make the exercise harder: walk your feet farther away from the wall. To make it easier: move your feet closer to the wall. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Arc’teryx Wants the Sperro SV to Be the Last Jacket You Ever Buy—Seriously
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.99
Engineered for versatility across high-stakes mountain environments, the Sperro SV underwent rigorous testing during ski tours and ice climbing ascents. (Photo: Courtesy of Arc'teryx) Tucked alongside the interior chest pocket of a two-toned magenta Arc’teryx jacket is a laser-etched QR code—but instead of pulling up the menu at your local pub, it prompts you to register your new purchase, immediately kicking off a record of the jacket’s materials, origin, and, eventually, repair history. A QR code seems simple enough—after all, you encounter dozens of them weekly—but a QR code on a mountain-grade hardshell requires a different level of engineering than the laminated square on your bartop. The internal placement makes it near-impossible to destroy or remove; the laser etching, adapted from the electronics industry, underwent multiple trials to ensure it left a permanent mark without degrading the fabric. So why spend so much time, money, and engineering on a single square inch of jacket? For Arc’teryx, that QR code is the entry point into System 0™, a new framework that reimagines how products can be designed, manufactured, used, repaired, and ultimately regenerated. In fact, the QR code is just one of many updates and innovations Arc’teryx built into its first System 0 jacket, the Sperro SV. Among the others: an easily repairable zipper, a nylon face fabric and backer engineered for chemical recyclability, and reinforcement at common failure points. System 0 started as a “what if” conversation between Arc’teryx CEO Stuart Haselden and VP of Advanced Concepts, Alex Plante, brainstorming what circularity would look like for the company. At that point, Arc’teryx’s ReBIRD program already existed, with a solid infrastructure for product repairs, resale, trade-in, and upcycling, but the team knew they were still missing an actual process—a viable, repeatable way to create products that can be used for longer and ultimately regenerated into something new. “We landed on what product we wanted to develop within that [circularity] concept, and then, while we were developing the product, realized that we didn’t have all the pieces of the system,” says Andrew Yip, Senior Director of Materials Innovation at Arc’teryx. That meant building capability as they went, bringing in people like Kyle Wood, Vice President of Strategy, to focus on circularity. They also recruited for other supporting roles, like sourcing manager for raw materials. Throughout the circularity initiative, Yip and his colleagues used one principle as their North Star: Sustainability alone isn’t a reason for a product to exist. Anything they created had to live up to Arc’teryx’s sky-high standards for technical excellence and durability. “Most sustainable materials and products are just less bad than their incumbent,” argues Yip. “If you’re just going to make something less bad from a sustainability perspective but make it worse in terms of performance, then there really isn’t a justification for it to exist.” To that end, Arc’teryx prioritized abrasion resistance on both face fabric and backer, while refusing to compromise on tear and tensile strength, waterproofing, and breathability—all the things that determine whether a jacket becomes a one-season purchase or a mainstay in your gear closet. They also intentionally aligned on nylon 6 as the key material instead of polyester; even though polyester has more recycling opportunities, the team knew that nylon 6 fabric would perform best. To find the exact nylon content ratio—the perfect number that would make the fabric functionally and financially recyclable—Arc’teryx worked closely with Aquafil, the manufacturer of ECONYL® regenerated nylon. According to Aquafil, the textile is known for high wear resistance and impact strength (aka extreme durability). Finding the perfect jacket material was one thing. But that wasn’t the hardest problem the Arc’teryx team had to solve, says Yip. You already know Arc’teryx for its insanely technical, single-purpose shells like the Alpha SV—a scalpel, according to Yip. “It’s really a precision tool, and it was designed for ice climbing,” he explains. “It doesn’t have hand pockets for a reason—you don’t need hand pockets when you’re ice climbing.” On the contrary, the Sperro SV had to be a jacket-of-all-trades, working in a variety of environments and use cases. “With the Sperro SV, we wanted to make something that was multi-environment, multifunctional, and multi-activity,” details Yip. They needed a Swiss Army Knife, not a scalpel—but that Swiss Army Knife couldn’t compromise on durability. To ensure the Sperro SV was worth its mettle, Arc’teryx tested the jacket on ski tours, hiking trips, snowshoeing expeditions, and even ice climbing. They also partnered with the North Shore Search and Rescue, a volunteer-led organization and one of Canada’s oldest search-and-rescue teams, to make sure the jacket performed in high-stakes scenarios. All that engineering ultimately serves one purpose: creating a jacket worthy of what Yip refers to as custodianship, rather than ownership. “Hopefully, the person who’s purchasing this jacket is somebody who cares about their stuff and is going to take care of the garment, bring it in for repair, and extend its lifetime as much as possible,” says Yip. “And only after many, many years and many, many repairs, when something is no longer repairable, only then is when we take it back.” Hence, the QR code. Arc’teryx hopes that by making it as seamless as possible for customers to track the Sperro SV’s lifespan, materials, and repair history, customers will view themselves as custodians with a responsibility to their gear—instead of temporary owners of a disposable item. If all goes according to plan, the Sperro SV might be the last jacket Arc’teryx ever sells you. At a gulp-worthy $1,200 retail price, most customers are probably praying that they never have to buy another jacket again, but it’s not exactly a sound business strategy in an industry that counts on customers to replace old gear. Yip is strangely okay with that. “When we’re developing new products and prototypes, we know we have something when our athletes and field testers don’t want to give it back,” he explains. “Similarly, I think we’re onto something if we have a commercial product that people can buy and they don’t want to replace it. So personally, I would have no problem with that.” When asked to comment on the price, Arc’teryx reps note that the Sperro SV is priced in line with their most advanced hard shells, and the price reflects the design effort and materials that went into this sustainable jacket. “Circularity at this level of performance requires significant investment across materials, manufacturing, certification, and end-of-life infrastructure,” Arc’teryx acknowledges. They believe that the price reflects the value of three years of unlimited repairs, a product they’re backing to last for years, and eventually, an end-of-life offramp. “When you factor in the total life of the jacket, the value calculation looks different than a traditional purchase,” reasons the brand. Whether consumers will find the price a fair trade-off for the total package remains to be seen. The Sperro SV is just the first “statement of intent,” as Yip puts it, for what System 0 can do within the Arc’teryx playbook. With the streamlined processes and internal philosophies Arc’teryx has now aligned on, they’re free to explore further iterations of circular gear. “We started with a hardshell because it’s what we know, what we make, and what we’re known for—so you can imagine that the other things we’re known for and make well are coming down the pipeline,” hints Yip. And for the Arc’teryx loyalists who worry this new iteration of a hardshell won’t live up to their high standards—you’ve got nothing to worry about. “If anyone were to put on the jacket and close their eyes, it really shouldn’t be different at all compared to anything that we’ve made before. And I think that’s the point,” says Yip. “It’s everything else around it that we’re trying to change.”

item.title: Marmots Are Having a Moment and I’m Here for It
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.06
Marmots are having a moment (Photo: Getty Images) What’s chubby, hairy, and likes to lick rocks? No—it’s not a typical Pacific Crest Trail thru-hiker. I’m of course referring to a marmot, the cute and cuddly high-alpine critter that’s currently taking the internet by storm. Marmots are having a moment, and I couldn’t be happier. If you’re like me, then your social media algorithm this month has overflowed with adorable marmot content. My personal marmot deep dive began in mid-August when an outdoor influencer named Jared Shult posted this video of a particularly charismatic marmot at Mount Rainier National Park hugging his leg. Shult recorded himself petting and stroking the marmot, and was subsequently fined $230 for doing so. National Park Service rules specifically prohibit visitors from touching wild animals—even the cute ones. Oops! Shult’s video had auspicious timing, as it hit social media just before Colorado’s inaugural Fat Marmot Week, a highly entertaining online contest operated by the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory’s (RMBL) Marmot Project. Much like Fat Bear Week, the RMBL, which studies marmots outside of Crested Butte, Colorado, asked fans to vote between eight yellow-bellied marmots who were trying to gain the most weight before winter. The winner, a particularly chonky marmot named Dawn, gained 4.5 pounds (about half his body weight) over the summer. Between Shult’s video and Fat Marmot Week, I’ve now consumed a vast array of marmot content. Marmots licking GoPro cameras. Marmots hugging. Marmots munching on rocks? I have awww‘d and ohhhh’d my way through all of the video clips showing these sentient stuffed animals doing cute little human things with their paws. I also learned that, like all critters, marmots are undomesticated wild animals driven by instincts and hunger, and, if given the chance, they may ruin your afternoon. The Wall Street Journal published a story accusing marmots of “terrorizing” guests in California’s Sequoia National Park by licking hikers, stealing their shoes, and occasionally breaking into their vehicles. The WSJ reporters also point out that marmots will sometimes crawl into the engine compartments of a parked car and devour cables, wires and hoses. My newfound marmot interest left me with more questions than answers. So, I recently sought some info from the global expert on the critters: Professor Daniel Blumstein of the Department of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology at the University of California, Los Angeles. Blumstein also oversees the Marmot Project at the RMBL, and spends his summers studying the cuddly critters near Gothic, Colorado. Here are some takeaways I got from our correspondence. OK, so that marmot didn’t crawl into the engine compartment of your Dodge Stratus looking to strand you at the trailhead parking lot. The critter was just really inquisitive—one of the familiar traits of the species, Blumstein told me. It’s the same reason why that marmot went up to Shult in Mount Rainier National Park. It wanted food. It wasn’t afraid. And, by nature, it wanted to investigate the situation. Alas, this curiosity can sometimes get marmots in trouble. Blumstein has seen marmots crawl into cars in Colorado and then go for an unplanned adventure. “One made it to the Phoenix area a few years ago and had to be flown back,” he said. “Once in a car, havoc sometimes results.” Those videos of marmots licking boulders and chewing pebbles are pretty weird, right? Well, it turns out the critters are on a lifelong quest to consume salt. A marmot’s normal diet of grasses and meadows that grow in alpine tundra leaves them salt-deficient, so they seek the stuff out wherever they can. Sometimes that means licking mineralized salt out of rocks. Blumstein believes that may also explain why some marmots venture into cars. “I’m told that radiator fluid tastes salty to animals,” he said. “It’s also possible that radiator hoses taste good to them!” This year the RMBL experienced a tragic die-off of marmots—the biggest since scientists started studying them outside of Crested Butte. Of the 160 marmots the group was studying, 100 died during the winter of 2025-26. This die-off corresponded with Colorado’s thinnest snowpack in more than 40 years. Blumstein and his team know that the die-off and dismal snow levels are related. Like many mountain mammals, marmots hibernate over the winter. And sometimes, many of the marmots that go to sleep in the fall never wake up in the spring. “Snow is insulation, so the snowpack acts as a blanket to keep the marmots warm over the winter,” he said. “It’s possible that those who were more likely to die were colder this year because they had less of a snowpack covering them.” Alas, the life of a marmot is full of dangers and pitfalls. Too deep of a snowpack can also spell certain doom for a marmot. They may starve to death while waiting for the melting snow to unearth the grass and flowers. Or, predators can pick them off while digging out of their burrows. “We’ve seen both happen in heavy snow years,” Blumstein added. Perhaps my favorite marmot fact involves the long sleep that the critters take during the winter. Like bears, marmots must fatten up in the late summer and fall to build up fat storage for the winter. But a marmot’s body is a miracle of efficiency once it is inactive. Yellow-bellied marmots will burn just a paperclip’s weight of fat a day when they’re hibernating. And during this time, Blumstein said, the marmot is not physiologically aging. “Hibernation is a secret to longevity,” Blumstein said. “Except that to live longer you have to miss ski season.” Blumstein’s favorite marmot trait is that the same individual critters generally return to the same trailheads, mountain meadows, and rocky slopes year after year. So, should the marmot that hugged Shult survive the cruel winter, he will probably be back at Mount Rainier to hug guests in 2027 and beyond. Just reminding everyone—don’t hug him back. For those of us who are drawn in by their cuddly ways, just know that even researchers feel the same way. “Plus, they look like little buddhas,” Blumstein added.

item.title: The High-Altitude Journey of the World’s Most Famous Adventure Cat
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.75
Simon the adventure cat (Photo: Courtesy of JJ Yosh) Had JJ Yosh, an adventure content creator based in Boulder, Colorado, simply taken his cat, Simon, on a handful of hikes and posted the videos online, I would have dismissed it as a pet-thetic social media stunt. But a decade after adopting the black Bombay cat, the duo—better known to millions as Backpacking Kitty on Instagram and TikTok—has built something far more remarkable. Together they’ve hiked the Austrian Alps, whitewater rafted California’s Sacramento River, climbed a volcano in Guatemala, and traveled to more than 15 countries and four continents. They’ve flown on over 100 flights, including on a seaplane, and kayaked some of the most remote waterways in the world, taking an audience of 11 million followers along with them, and making Simon less of a novelty and more like a bona fide field companion. Now Yosh has something even more ambitious in mind. He’s preparing to take Simon on a multi-year Seven Summits spree. “I’m positive he’s the only cat who has summited a dozen of Colorado’s 14ers,” Yosh says of Simon who he rescued from euthanasia in 2016. Yet even those accomplishments, and, arguably, the title of one of the most famous cats in the world, pale beside this latest odyssey. Over the next three years, they plan to tackle the tallest mountain on every continent: Denali, Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua, Mount Elbrus, Vinson Massif, Puncak Jaya, and the world’s highest peak, Mount Everest. Before you picture a cat being hauled into Everest’s notorious Death Zone—a place so hostile to life it contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level—rest easy. “I’m definitely not taking Simon to the summit. I’m not risking his life,” Yosh says. While Yosh makes his push for the top, Simon will be living the considerably cushier life at Everest Base Camp with a dedicated pet sitter, people he already knows and trusts. Yosh is emphatic that Simon’s health and safety come first. “How high he goes depends entirely on the mountain,” Yosh says. That means, for Everest, Base Camp is his ceiling. “Nothing above it, no exceptions.” For Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua? Those are non-technical walk-ups, so there is more room. “He could go higher than base camp on those, and how much higher gets decided on the ground rather than promised in advance.” As for everywhere else, Yosh will assess each peak one at a time, and veterinary opinions will inform each decision. Yosh says, “ If the answer is that it is too high for a cat, that is the end of it. He does not go.” It’s all part of the careful balance Yosh has spent the past decade striking with his feline partner. Simon may be born for adventure—while he does trek via leash, he’s happiest riding Yosh’s shoulders through forests and across alpine trails, even snowboarding—he’s still a cat, with very real limitations. For example, while Yosh was on a Mount Baker crevasse rescue training ahead of his Seven Summits bid recently, Simon wasn’t practicing self-arrests. Which begs the question: How do you prepare a house cat for extreme altitude? After all, Everest Base Camp sits at a breath-stealing 17,598 feet. The answer starts at home. In Boulder, where the pair live at roughly 6,000 feet above sea level, acclimatization is woven into everyday life. Yosh’s home—playfully known as “the house his cat built”—is tucked into a rocky cliff and outfitted with an indoor climbing wall scaled by both owner and pet. Outside, Colorado’s high country is Simon’s natural conditioning ground, where regular mountaineering outings have gradually exposed him to thinner air—one might say the purrfect conditions—long before the Himalayas come into view. Yosh has even taken Simon on technical rope climbs, securing him a small-dog harness. And when it comes to gear, Simon is just as outfitted as his owner: Yosh has assembled a wardrobe for Simon to rival any serious adventurer’s, with specialized gear for seemingly every climate, condition, and expedition. Add to that the deep relationship these two have built. Even talking about the possibility of something happening to Simon makes Yosh visibly shaken. The depth of that bond was forged early. Not long after Yosh adopted Simon, he left the cat with a friend while filming a commercial in Bolivia. What Yosh didn’t learn until later was that Simon had gone missing for three days. “Thankfully, they didn’t tell me at the time,” Yosh says. “They’d put up missing posters everywhere, but I had no idea.” Even now, the memory rattles him. “If that happened today and I found out while I was on a mountain, I’d turn around. I wouldn’t be able to finish the climb,” he says. “You have to be in a good mental place to climb a mountain, and I wouldn’t be.” “This work can be so taxing and draining. You question why you’re doing it over and over again,” Yosh says. “That’s where having Simon is such a huge emotional pillow. The hardest moments usually aren’t the scary, high-adrenaline ones. They’re when the weight of the whole expedition catches up with you.” Whether he’s just finished an ultrarun or a grueling climb, Yosh knows there’s one constant: Simon, curled up in the tent ready for a cuddle at the end of the day. In a life all about relentless forward motion, that ritual has become the reset that keeps him going. It will be tested during their next challenge. But first, there are the logistics to work through. Namely, the travel concerns of hop-scotching the planet with a cat. Fortunately, this isn’t Simon’s first rodeo. He has a U.S. ID card and an E.U. pet passport that allows him to easily cross borders, and he doesn’t fly cargo. “But of course he has to get all of these health certificates for each country,” Yosh says. Then there’s the tricky reality of lengthy flights and layovers. Naturally, I had to ask, does Simon get jet lag? “Simon gets so excited every time we reach a new hotel or destination,” Yosh says. “He’s like ready to go.” Apparently, when you’re an international adventuring cat of mystery, the only thing tougher than Everest is waiting for room service. That, and then clawing your way into mountaineering history.

item.title: Where to Stay in Moab, From Dirtbag Cheap (and Free) to Desert Luxury
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.61
The massage caves inside a sandstone formation at ULUM Moab, glamping at its peak. (Photo: Maya Silver) On my very first trip to Moab at age 10, I stayed at a very memorable hotel called the Gonzo Inn. I formed indelible memories of the hotel sign adorned with a clothed lizard straight out of the 1998 film (and 1972 novel) Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and of a sunlit glorious pool—a reprieve from the hot, dry days of Southeastern Utah. This little lodge had just opened in 1998; the town was rather quiet back then. Nearly three decades later, the Gonzo Inn is still there every time I return to Moab, which is approximately twice a year when I can get away from my home in northern Utah a few hours away. In my dozens of pilgrimages to the desert, I’ve stayed just about everywhere you can imagine in the adventure capital of Utah (and arguably the Southwest). I’ve pulled over on the side of BLM roads at dusk, set up my tent in sandy dispersed campsites, started campfires that cast shadows against stone, settled for budget hotel rooms in tighter times, booked Airbnbs and VRBOs for large crews, and splurged on lodges right on the Colorado River. If you’re headed to Moab, I’ve put together my personal guide to where to bed down between adventures. From Free 99 to $1,200, here’s the best places to stay in Moab for every budget, the pros and cons of each spot, and some insider tips. My favorite Moab trips often include a mix of camping with a splurge night or two at a hotel. Keep in mind that availability and rates fluctuate dramatically depending on the season. Though these days, winter (December through February) is just about the only time Moab isn’t busy. During the rest of the year, make reservations well in advance. In winter, rates typically drop 40 percent, and during spring break season, prices tend to rise. If you know where to look, you can find free dispersed camping on BLM land to park your van or pitch your tent around Moab. A popular spot where I used to camp was once along U.S. 191 heading into town. But the new Utahraptor State Park has turned some of the dispersed camping into two campgrounds. You can still access dispersed camping beyond the Dalton Wells Dinosaur Quarry to the east, or further south near the Klonzo and Sovereign trailheads, but you’ll need to enter the state park to get there. If you want to avoid a fee, you can try sweet talking the state park ranger, or entering at odd hours when the entrance is unmanned. You can also find some dispersed camping along La Sal Mountain Loop Road. This is an especially great option in late spring through early fall, when the mountains are the place to escape the heat. Check out this map to see where the BLM land that allows dispersed camping exists—and where camping is explicitly banned. Location: Across the Moab area Pros: Free peace and quiet Cons: May require some questing Local tip: Buy some wag bags at a local gear shop (like Gearheads Outdoor Store) to responsibly dispose of your human waste. It can take 10 or more years to break down in the desert, so digging a deep hole ain’t cutting it. You can dispose of those wag bags in trash receptacles marked accordingly in downtown Moab. If you’re on a dirtbag budget but need a roof over your head—maybe you don’t have camping gear or maybe it’s cold and rainy—head to Moab’s only hostel. In full transparency, I have not stayed at Lazy Lizard Hostel. But I have stayed at many hostels and I included this one in my Moon travel guide to Utah because I’ve heard great things (it also has 4.5 stars on Google with over 700 reviews). This locally owned hostel has been around since 1987 and 40 years later, it’s still a great place to rent a room in Moab for as cheap as possible. If you’d rather not bunk down with strangers, you can pay a bit more ($48) for a two-person guest room, or a log cabin ($53-70; sleeps up to six). Location: 1 mile south of town Pros: Dirt cheap Cons: Not walking distance to town Local tip: Bring coins. If you’re dirtbagging it, chances are your clothes stink as much as you do! Use the coin-operated laundry machines onsite. Devils Garden Campground in Arches National Park is one of my favorite spots to camp anywhere. For one, it positions you to catch sunrises, sunsets, and stars amid the arches—and without the crowds. Humps and hills of slickrock roll upward right from the campsites. And a lovely trail to Broken Arch starts right from the campground. Reserve as far in advance as you can, or come during the first-come, first-served off season (Nov.-Feb.)—and bring a lot of layers. Plan a sunrise or sunset hike to Delicate Arch while you’re sleeping in the area. Bathrooms and potable water are available, but there are no hook-ups and you can’t buy firewood here. Also if you’d rather not cook at camp, it’s easy to pick up takeout or pre-made food at Moonflower Co-op in town and bring it up to your campsite. Location: In the Devils Garden area of Arches National Park, about 22 miles north of Moab Pros: Arches within spitting distance of your tent Cons: Hard to get a reservation Local tip: Reservations may be difficult to come by in peak season, but this campground is first come, first served from November through February. Roll up in the morning and snag a site. If you can’t find a site, Sand Flats Recreation Area on a hill just east of Moab offers similarly scenic campsites—and dinosaur tracks. Aside from camping, hostels, and chain motels, the most reasonable rates and best stay in Moab can be found at The Gonzo Inn, where I first stayed in 1999. This locally owned hotel just a block from Main Street offers standard rooms and condo-style suites, plus a lovely outdoor pool and firepit area. Inspired by the hallucinatory lizards of Fear and Loathing, the vibe is colorful, convivial, and “desert chic,” as Gonzo describes itself. Hunter S. Thompson would surely approve. Location: One block west of Main St. Pros: Rooms include a $14 breakfast voucher per person per day. Cons: The onsite cafe where you can use that voucher was very crowded with long lines the last time I stayed here. Local tip: The hotel offers secure gear storage for your dirty bike; ask at the front desk. Just a few miles drive down the road from Sorrel River Ranch, Red Cliffs Lodge has hosted guests along the Colorado River since the 1980s, but the ranch of the same name has been here since the 19th century. The lodge has changed hands many times; most recently, it was acquired by Marriott and dramatically renovated. In the basement of the lodge, you’ll find the Moab Museum of Film & Western Heritage, which has long housed a collection of memorabilia from Westerns filmed in Moab. In fact, many films have been shot right at Red Cliffs, including Wagon Master, Son of Cochise, Warlock, and the John Wayne film Rio Grande. With its can’t-beat-it location right on the Colorado, one of the best perks about Red Cliffs is that you can book a rafting or SUPing trip through the property. Many of the accommodations are in well-sized and well-appointed cabins, and many come with river views. The decor feels more modern than what you’ll find at Sorrel River Ranch. There is also a New American restaurant onsite called Ember with a swanky (for Moab) lounge and a patio overlooking the Colorado. Red Cliffs is pricey, but if you want to balance a long day of roughing it on the trails or river with a luxury stay, this is my favorite place to do it. It’s cheaper to stay in the main lodge ($225-600), then to get a cabin ($1,000-$1,200 per night). Location: In Grandstaff Canyon along Highway 191, 17 miles northeast of Moab Pros: The sights and sound of the Colorado River right outside your room. Cons: If you want to be in town, it’s a 30-minute drive to Moab. Local tip: Red Cliffs is just a stone’s throw away from Castle Valley. Cool off and take a scenic drive up into the La Sal Mountains, where you can hike, bike, climb, or just bask in the big views. You’ve probably heard of Under Canvas, the network of stargazing-focused glamping across the country, often adjacent to national parks. But you may not have heard of the slightly more luxury-oriented ULUM, which opened in 2023 by the same folks behind Under Canvas. At ULUM Moab, every tent is a “suite” with its own bathroom. But more importantly, the ULUM Moab location is approximately 10 times more lovely than the Under Canvas Moab location, which sits right off Highway 191 amid wind-blown sagebrush lands. By comparison, ULUM Moab is about a 30-minute drive south of Moab, tucked in a wind-protected ring of stunning sandstone cliffs. It’s also within spitting distance of the Looking Glass rock feature—a magnificent arch that offers hiking, scrambling, rock climbing, and rappelling. I’ve stayed at Under Canvas Moab and luckily, had a tent with a bathroom. But as far as I’m concerned, if I’m going to dish out a few hundred dollars to glamp, the setting better be spectacular (rather than windy and shade-less) and I want my own bathroom. Otherwise, I’d rather pitch my own tent. And I don’t want to pay $200-$500 with the sound of said wind rattling the metal bones of the canvas tent, keeping me up all night. ULUM also offers some noteworthy amenities like a literal massage cave, a pretty decent onsite restaurant, and warm/cold plunge pools. ULUM Moab is open late-March through late-October. Location: 25 miles south of Moab, off Highway 191 Pros: In a remote location, the stars here are absolutely next-level. Especially against the backdrop of Looking Glass Rock. Cons: It’s a 30-minute drive from Arches and Moab, with no restaurants or shops nearby. Local tip: ULUM Moab makes for a great basecamp to climb, hike, and explore nearby Indian Creek, the Newspaper Rock Petroglyph Panel, and the Needles District of Canyonlands. It’s also a good spot to stop for a night en route to destinations further south like Bears Ears National Monument or Monument Valley. You can’t beat the setting: Sorrel River Ranch sits right on the Colorado River. I should add that this lodge did have a little drama in the news recently, when the state temporarily shut it down over violations in its onsite water treatment system. The lodge has since reopened and vehemently denied some concerning allegations that restaurant workers were asked to use pool water to wash dishes(!). I stayed at Sorrel River Ranch—a couple months before the water issues bubbled up—for my son’s birthday and thankfully, all of our digestive systems during our stay were fine. All of the rooms here are in big log cabins, some with two floors. The decor is Westerncore with touches like a rodeo lasso passing as art, bull’s horns hanging on the walls, a bed made of logs, and housemade red, white, and blue chips with salsa as a welcome offering. Book a horseback ride, enroll your kids in the junior wrangler program, or just feed the boisterous goats. Location: In Grandstaff Canyon along Highway 191, 20 miles northeast of Moab Pros: Serene location close to trails, climbing, and the Colorado River Local tip: Sorrel Ranch sits 10 minutes away from the trailhead to Fisher Towers. This rollicking hike meanders over rock ledges and through gullies as it takes in stunning rock formations—peep the iconic Ancient Art tower, a classic climbing testpiece. About the author: Maya Silver has been traveling to Moab since 1999. These are only a handful of the places she’s stayed in Moab, but they are her favorites. Even though Moab has become almost unbearably busy at times in the 27 years since she’s been visiting, she still loves this bustling adventure town of Southeastern Utah. When she isn’t acting as editor-in-chief of Climbing Magazine, she also writes Moon travel guides to Utah, including a just-updated edition of her guide to Southern Utah.

item.title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.49
Nantes, France As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun. On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks. This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life. The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste. Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic. Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff. All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits. And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve. Joanne O’Connor The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January. Basel, Switzerland Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend. Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine. Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines. But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design. Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023. That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch. Max Benato The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only Lübeck, Germany Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem. The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires. Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace. But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore. To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937. In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015). We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer. Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back. In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash. Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort. Rachel Dixon The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only Parma, Italy Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio. The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free. Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds. Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect. This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15. John Brunton Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only Santander, Spain Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map. Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times. With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield. Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America. Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half. Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre. The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas. After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander. The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too. Eddi Fiegel The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

item.title: ‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.51
Renaissance art without the crowds in Italy Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna won me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel near Via delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. The Palazzo dei Diamanti was almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkin cappellacci, a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty. John One of Germany’s greenest cities Next to flashy Munich or cool Berlin, Hanover in northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallery Sprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – the Great Garden at Herrenhausen – impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multicultural Linden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at the Teestübchen. Ulrike The Algarve’s city of crafts Bursting with Portuguese charm, Loulé is 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported by Loulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations. Sue Unesco sites in northern France Arras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: the belfry of the Hotel de Ville and the Vauban Citadel. Exploring the Boves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods. Bryan Boese Artistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful south Malmö is easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. The Western Harbour contains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraper Turning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafe Hollandia offered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. The Disgusting Food Museum next door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)! Elisabeth Brilliant beach and seafood in Sardinia If you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love in Cagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark of Bastione St Remy delineating the ancient Castello district and serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, and Trattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back. Martha Stained glass wonder in north-west Spain In León, colours grab your attention and take away words. León cathedral completely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-century San Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast. Deborah Norway’s art nouveau gem Ålesund is one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramic Aksla mountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunning Geirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all! Teresa Stansby The French city with a bit of everything I spent five days in Saint-Malo this August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (on Instagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C. Sophie Amos Winning tip: a watery Dutch master of a city Leiden starts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls. Bill Jones Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

Highest welcome offer The highest welcome offer we've seen for the Citi / AAdvantage Business World Elite Mastercard was when it gave new cardholders the opportunity to earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first five months of account opening. Learn more: Citi / AAdvantage Business World Elite Mastercard Application restrictions Citi has some strict application restrictions. Citi doesn't limit the number of cards you can have, but it will limit your overall credit. Citi is also sensitive to recent inquiries, so for the best results, wait a few months from your last card application before applying for a Citi card. Additionally, Citi has the 8/65 rule, which means: - You can apply for only one card (personal or business) every eight days and no more than two cards in a 65-day window. - You can only apply for one business card every 90 days. There are exceptions to this rule, but this is general guidance for optimal results. You'll generally want a good credit score of at least 670 before applying for either card. Additionally, if you have previously earned a welcome bonus on a Citi / AAdvantage card, it's possible to earn another. According to the Citi / AA Executive's terms, "New account bonus is not available if you have received a new account bonus for a Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive account in the past 48 months or if you converted another Citi credit card account on which you earned a new account bonus in the last 48 months into a Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive account." These terms apply only to individual cards, not to the whole family of cards. You can also hold multiple Citi / AA cards at the same time. You can even earn multiple welcome bonuses as long as they are different card products and it's outside the 48-month window. It's important to note that the 48-month period starts when you receive the welcome bonus, not when you're approved for the card. For example, if you switch to the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard after earning the welcome bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard, you'd still have to wait 48 months from when you earned your welcome bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive to earn another Citi / AAdvantage Executive welcome bonus. Related: What you need to know about earning another American Airlines card welcome bonus Bottom line Before applying for a Citi / AAdvantage credit card, make sure you're getting the best possible welcome bonus. Our historical data on welcome offers can serve as a reference point for determining the best time to apply for Citi / AA cards, based on year-over-year trends.
